D265ACD0DFE401311D3468A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast the materials used by humans and animals to build shelters.

D2656D00DFE401311D3368A86D17958E.description: Seek information in books, magazines and pictures that describes materials used to build shelters by people in different regions of the world.

D26516A0DFE401311D3268A86D17958E.description: Conduct simple tests to compare the properties of different materials and their usefulness for making roofs, windows, walls or floors (e.g., waterproof, transparent, strong).

D264D8E0DFE401311D3168A86D17958E.description:
Some objects are natural, while others have been designed and made by people to improve the quality of life.
This content standard is an application of the concepts in content standard K.1 and should be integrated into the same unit.

D2645980DFE401311D2F68A86D17958E.description: Make judgments about appropriate clothing and activities based on weather conditions.

D26418E0DFE401311D2E68A86D17958E.description: Write, speak or draw ways that weather influences humans, other animals and plants.

D263D900DFE401311D2D68A86D17958E.description: Observe, compare and contrast cloud shapes, sizes and colors, and relate the appearance of clouds to fair weather or precipitation.

D2639010DFE401311D2C68A86D17958E.description: Analyze weather data collected over time (during the day, from day to day, and from season to season) to identify patterns and make comparisons and predictions.

D2634960DFE401311D2B68A86D17958E.description: Use the senses to observe daily weather conditions and record data systematically using organizers such as tables, charts, picture graphs or calendars.

D26307F0DFE401311D2A68A86D17958E.description: Weather conditions vary daily and seasonally.

D26288F0DFE401311D2868A86D17958E.description: Recognize varied individuals as examples of the same kind of living thing (e.g., different color rabbits are all rabbits; different breeds of dogs are all dogs).

D2623FF0DFE401311D2768A86D17958E.description: Match pictures or models of adults with their offspring (animals and plants).

D261D980DFE401311D2668A86D17958E.description: Observe and write, speak or draw about similarities and differences between plants and animals.

D25BF0A0DFE401311D2568A86D17958E.description: Use nonstandard measures to estimate and compare the height, length or weight of different kinds of plants and animals.

D25BB670DFE401311D2468A86D17958E.description: Sort and count living and nonliving things in the classroom, the schoolyard and in pictures.

D25B7BE0DFE401311D2368A86D17958E.description: Observe and describe differences between living and nonliving things in terms of growth, offspring and need for energy from "food."

D25B3FB0DFE401311D2268A86D17958E.description: Many different kinds of living things inhabit the Earth.

D25ABE90DFE401311D2068A86D17958E.description: Count, order and sort objects by their observable properties.

D25A7270DFE401311D1F68A86D17958E.description: Describe properties of materials such as wood, plastic, metal, cloth or paper and sort objects by the material from which they are made.

D25A3640DFE401311D1E68A86D17958E.description: Use simple tools and nonstandard units to estimate or predict properties such as size, heaviness, magnetic attraction and float/sink.

D259F940DFE401311D1D68A86D17958E.description: Classify organisms or objects by one and two observable properties and explain the rule used for sorting (e.g., size, color, shape, texture or flexibility).

D259BAA0DFE401311D1C68A86D17958E.description: Make scientific observations using the five senses, and distinguish between an object's observable properties and its name or its uses.

D2597C90DFE401311D1B68A86D17958E.description: Match each of the five senses with its associated body part and the kind of information it perceives.

D2593D60DFE401311D1A68A86D17958E.description: Objects have properties that can be observed and used to describe similarities and differences.

document.title: Connecticut Social Studies Curriculum Framework

D3D31BB0DFE401311FF868A86D17958E.description: recognize that money is a generally accepted medium of exchange and that different countries use different currencies.

D3D2D5E0DFE401311FF768A86D17958E.description: describe how the exchange of goods and services around the world creates interdependence among people in different places; and

D3D29420DFE401311FF668A86D17958E.description: describe how voluntary exchange benefits all parties involved in the exchange of goods and services;

D3D24FA0DFE401311FF568A86D17958E.description: Students will demonstrate how the exchange of goods and services by individuals, groups and nations creates economic interdependence and how trade results in change. Educational experiences will assure that students:

D3D1C1A0DFE401311FF368A86D17958E.description: explain that government raises money by taxing and borrowing to pay for the goods and services it provides.

D3D174C0DFE401311FF268A86D17958E.description: explain that some goods and services are provided by the government; and

D3D11D70DFE401311FF168A86D17958E.description: describe how the price of a good or service in a market is related to how much of it there is and how many people want it;

D3D0D650DFE401311FF068A86D17958E.description: define a consumer and a producer and their roles in a market system;

D3D09330DFE401311FEF68A86D17958E.description: explain that a market exists whenever buyers and sellers exchange goods and services;

D3D05040DFE401311FEE68A86D17958E.description: explain that there are different economic systems in the world and that these systems use different means to produce, distribute and exchange goods and services;

D3D00B30DFE401311FED68A86D17958E.description: identify the three basic questions all economic systems must answer: What will be produced? How will it be produced? For whom will it be produced?;

D3CFBF60DFE401311FEC68A86D17958E.description: Students will demonstrate that various economic systems coexist, and that economic decisions are made by individuals and/or governments, influenced by markets, cultural traditions, individuals and governments in the allocation of goods and services. Educational experiences will assure that students:

D3CF1AC0DFE401311FEA68A86D17958E.description: identify alternative uses of resources found in their home, school or neighborhood.

D3CED0B0DFE401311FE968A86D17958E.description: explain why some countries are richer than others; and

D3CE83F0DFE401311FE868A86D17958E.description: identify and give examples of resources: human, natural and capital, and explain how they are used;

D3CE3880DFE401311FE768A86D17958E.description: identify goods and services and give an example of each;

D3CD9DF0DFE401311FE568A86D17958E.description: Students will demonstrate that because human, natural and capital resources are limited, individuals, households, businesses and governments must make choices. Educational experiences will assure that students:

D3CD0AA0DFE401311FE368A86D17958E.description: describe how and why physical and human systems function and interact and the consequences of these interactions.

D3CCB7D0DFE401311FE268A86D17958E.description: identify locations of various economic activities and understand how physical and human factors influence them; and

D3CC65E0DFE401311FE168A86D17958E.description: explain ways in which humans use and interact with environments;

D3CC0930DFE401311FE068A86D17958E.description: explain how human and natural processes shape places;

D3CBB4E0DFE401311FDF68A86D17958E.description: use maps, globes, graphs, models, computer programs and texts, as appropriate;

D3CB6B40DFE401311FDE68A86D17958E.description: create information from maps, globes and geographic models in graphs, diagrams and charts;

D3CB2430DFE401311FDD68A86D17958E.description: explain the characteristics and purposes of maps, globes and other geographical tools and technologies;

D3CADFF0DFE401311FDC68A86D17958E.description: Students will use geographic tools and technology to explain the interactions of humans and the larger environment, and the evolving consequences of those interactions. Educational experiences will assure that students:

D3CA4450DFE401311FDA68A86D17958E.description: locate major physical and human features in the New England region and the United States.

D3C9EFE0DFE401311FD968A86D17958E.description: locate places within their own and nearby communities in Connecticut; and

D3C9AB80DFE401311FD868A86D17958E.description: describe the characteristics of a physical and a human system;

D3C965F0DFE401311FD768A86D17958E.description: explain locations and characteristics of human settlements and how they have changed over time;

D3C91FA0DFE401311FD668A86D17958E.description: locate Earth's major physical and human features (including cities, countries, bodies of water, etc.);

D3C8DC50DFE401311FD568A86D17958E.description: understand the elements of culture and how they change;

D3C89230DFE401311FD468A86D17958E.description: identify the political, social and economic units of an area;

D3C84380DFE401311FD368A86D17958E.description: explain the patterns, distributions and relocations of people;

D3C7FF80DFE401311FD268A86D17958E.description: Students will interpret spatial patterns of human migration, economic activities and political units in Connecticut, the nation and the world. Educational experiences will assure that students:

D3C76620DFE401311FD068A86D17958E.description: locate Earth's major physical and human features (including cities, countries, bodies of water, etc.).

D3C715F0DFE401311FCF68A86D17958E.description: draw a simple map of continents and oceans; and

D3C682F0DFE401311FCD68A86D17958E.description: explain the factors that affect the location, distribution and associations of features of the physical environment;

D3C63DB0DFE401311FCC68A86D17958E.description: demonstrate how Earth-sun relationships shape climate and vegetation patterns;

D3C5E1C0DFE401311FCB68A86D17958E.description: identify the types of physical systems and their characteristics that affect the Earth's surface;

D3C58D90DFE401311FCA68A86D17958E.description: Students will use spatial perspective to explain the physical processes that shape the Earth's surface and its ecosystems. Educational experiences will assure that students:

D3E7BC40DFE40131203B68A86D17958E.description: locate major physical and human features in the New England region and the United States.

D3E77A70DFE40131203A68A86D17958E.description: locate places within their own and nearby communities in Connecticut; and

D3E73770DFE40131203968A86D17958E.description: observe and describe how places and regions are identified, defined and bounded;

D3E6F000DFE40131203868A86D17958E.description: provide reasons why and describe how places and regions change and are connected;

D3E6A470DFE40131203768A86D17958E.description: explain how human and natural processes shape places;

D3E64FE0DFE40131203668A86D17958E.description: define and identify natural and human characteristics of places;

D3E60550DFE40131203568A86D17958E.description: Students will use spatial perspective to identify and analyze the significance of physical and cultural characteristics of places and world regions. Educational experiences will assure that students:

D3E572B0DFE40131203368A86D17958E.description: describe ways in which communities and nations influence each other.

D3E52F40DFE40131203268A86D17958E.description: explain how communities and nations interact with one another; and

D3E4E4A0DFE40131203168A86D17958E.description: Students will demonstrate an understanding of how the major elements of international relations and world affairs affect their lives and the security and well-being of their community, state and nation. Educational experiences will assure that students:

D3E44B40DFE40131202F68A86D17958E.description: explain that it is important to limit government so that individual rights can be protected.

D3E40250DFE40131202E68A86D17958E.description: identify what governments can and cannot do; and

D3E3A7D0DFE40131202D68A86D17958E.description: identify protection of individual rights and promotion of the common good;

D3E354F0DFE40131202C68A86D17958E.description: define and describe government in terms of people and groups who apply and enforce rules and laws;

D3E2F8D0DFE40131202B68A86D17958E.description: describe the need for a limited government so that people can be treated fairly;

D3E2A5B0DFE40131202A68A86D17958E.description: define power and authority and how they evolve into government;

D3E24EC0DFE40131202968A86D17958E.description: Students will explain that political systems emanate from the need of humans for order, leading to compromise and the establishment of authority. Educational experiences will assure that students:

D3E1C140DFE40131202768A86D17958E.description: exercise political participation by discussing public issues, building consensus and becoming involved in politics.

D3E17C80DFE40131202668A86D17958E.description: explain the importance of taking an active role in political leadership and public service in their school and community; and

D3E13090DFE40131202568A86D17958E.description: establish, explain and apply criteria useful in evaluating rules and laws for solving problems and resolving conflicts between people;

D3E0CAC0DFE40131202468A86D17958E.description: identify the rights of citizens in a democratic society and explain why certain responsibilities are important to themselves, their families, community, state and nation;

D3E07E20DFE40131202368A86D17958E.description: explain the meaning and important characteristics of citizenship in the United States;

D3E03410DFE40131202268A86D17958E.description: Students will demonstrate knowledge of the rights and responsibilities of citizens to participate in and shape public policy, and contribute to the maintenance of our democratic way of life. Educational experiences will assure that students:

D3DF9E80DFE40131202068A86D17958E.description: apply the concepts of liberty, tolerance and majority rule and how they relate to individual rights.

D3DF4980DFE40131201F68A86D17958E.description: identify the location of seats of government at the local, state and national levels; and

D3DEF640DFE40131201E68A86D17958E.description: apply the process of how leaders are selected and how people monitor and influence decisions of their government;

D3DEA2F0DFE40131201D68A86D17958E.description: identify services provided by national, state and local governments and how we pay for them through taxation;

D3DE4DB0DFE40131201C68A86D17958E.description: recognize the Constitution, including the Bill of Rights, as an important document that guides our country and limits the power of the government;

D3DDF870DFE40131201B68A86D17958E.description: explain that individuals have rights and responsibilities to follow the law;

D3DDA590DFE40131201A68A86D17958E.description: explain the purposes of laws and the ideas and principles that make just laws;

D3DD5350DFE40131201968A86D17958E.description: Students will apply knowledge of the U. S. Constitution, how the U. S. system of government works and how the rule of law and the values of liberty and equality have an impact on individual, local, state and national decisions. Educational experiences will assure that students:

D3DCB5F0DFE40131201768A86D17958E.description: recognize relationships between events and people of the past and present circumstances, concerns and developments.

D3DC46E0DFE40131201668A86D17958E.description: display empathy for people who have lived in the past; and

D3DBF0B0DFE40131201568A86D17958E.description: be active learners at cultural institutions, such as museums and historical exhibitions;

D3DB99C0DFE40131201468A86D17958E.description: seek historical background when confronted with problems and issues of the past, as well as of today's world and their own lives;

D3DB57C0DFE40131201368A86D17958E.description: exhibit curiosity and pose questions about the past when presented with artifacts, records or other evidence of the past;

D3DB13B0DFE40131201268A86D17958E.description: Students will recognize the continuing importance of historical thinking and historical knowledge in their own lives and in the world in which they live. Educational experiences will assure that students:

D3DA89A0DFE40131201068A86D17958E.description: identify individual achievements of scientists and inventors from many cultures and different historical periods and describe their achievements.

D3DA3760DFE40131200F68A86D17958E.description: describe the impact of various technological developments on the local community and on the nation; and

D3D9E130DFE40131200E68A86D17958E.description: describe some goods, products and ideas which were exchanged as the result of movement;

D3D98670DFE40131200D68A86D17958E.description: describe and explain some of the reasons people have moved and relate these reasons to some historic movements of large groups of people;

D3D92450DFE40131200C68A86D17958E.description: explain different types of conflict, different ways in which conflicts have been resolved, and different ways that conflicts and their resolutions have affected people;

D3D8DA40DFE40131200B68A86D17958E.description: examine family life and cultures of different peoples at different times in history;

D3D88FD0DFE40131200A68A86D17958E.description: recognize that people develop traditions that transmit their beliefs and ideals;

D3D83D80DFE40131200968A86D17958E.description: Students will apply their understanding of historical periods, issues and trends to examine such historical themes as ideals, beliefs and institutions; conflict and conflict resolution; human movement and interaction; and science and technology in order to understand how the world came to be the way it is. Educational experiences will assure that students:

D3D7B5D0DFE40131200768A86D17958E.description: place the history of their own families in the context of local, state, national and world history.

D3D76E00DFE40131200668A86D17958E.description: demonstrate knowledge of major trends in state and local history, including history of original peoples, early settlements and selected changes over the past two centuries; and

D3D724D0DFE40131200568A86D17958E.description: locate the events, peoples and places they have studied in time and place (e.g., on a time line and map) relative to their own location;

D3D6C130DFE40131200468A86D17958E.description: demonstrate a familiarity with peoples, events and places from a broad spectrum of human experience through selected study from historical periods and from the various regions (e.g., East Asia, Europe, the Americas, Africa, South Asia, West Asia);

D3D65470DFE40131200368A86D17958E.description: Students will use historical thinking skills to develop an understanding of the major historical periods, issues and trends in United States history, world history, and Connecticut and local history. Educational experiences will assure that students:

D3D61330DFE40131200268A86D17958E.description: Local, United States and World History

D3D5D0E0DFE40131200168A86D17958E.description: write short narratives and statements of historical ideas and create other appropriate presentations from investigations of source materials.

D3D58EA0DFE40131200068A86D17958E.description: create timelines which sequence events and peoples, using days, weeks, months, years, decades and centuries; and

D3D54A70DFE401311FFF68A86D17958E.description: identify ways different cultures record their histories, compare past and present situations and events, and present findings in appropriate oral, written and visual ways;

D3D50430DFE401311FFE68A86D17958E.description: identify the main idea in a source of historical information;

D3D45840DFE401311FFC68A86D17958E.description: engage in reading challenging primary and secondary historical source materials, some of which is contradictory and requires questioning of validity;

D3D40A80DFE401311FFB68A86D17958E.description: gather historical data from multiple sources;

D3D3BA60DFE401311FFA68A86D17958E.description: Students will develop historical thinking skills, including chronological thinking and recognizing change over time; contextualizing, comprehending and analyzing historical literature; researching historical sources; understanding the concept of historical causation; understanding competing narratives and interpretation; and constructing narratives and interpretation. Educational experiences will assure that students:

document.title: Connecticut Arts Curriculum Framework

DE000EB0DFE40131337368A86D17958E.description: recognize that works of visual art are produced by artisans and artists working in different cultures, times and places.

DDFFC0B0DFE40131337268A86D17958E.description: demonstrate understanding of how the visual arts are used in the world around us; and

DDFF7780DFE40131337168A86D17958E.description: describe how the visual arts are combined with other arts in multimedia work;

DDFF2150DFE40131337068A86D17958E.description: identify connections between the visual arts and other disciplines in the curriculum;

DDFECAD0DFE40131336F68A86D17958E.description: identify connections between characteristics of the visual arts and other arts disciplines;

DDFE6CA0DFE40131336E68A86D17958E.description: Students will make connections between the visual arts, other disciplines and daily life.

DDFB9740DFE40131336568A86D17958E.description: identify possible improvements in the process of creating their own work.

DDFB4300DFE40131336468A86D17958E.description: describe their personal responses to specific works of art using visual art terminology; and

DDFAF820DFE40131336368A86D17958E.description: recognize that there are different responses to specific works of art;

DDFAAC80DFE40131336268A86D17958E.description: describe visual characteristics of works of art using visual art terminology;

DDFA5DF0DFE40131336168A86D17958E.description: identify various purposes for creating works of art;

DDFA0520DFE40131336068A86D17958E.description: Students will reflect upon, describe, analyze, interpret and evaluate their own and others' work.

DDF23AC0DFE40131334868A86D17958E.description: create art work that demonstrates understanding of how history or culture can influence visual art.

DDF1E4B0DFE40131334768A86D17958E.description: identify specific works of art as belonging to particular styles, cultures, times and places; and

DDF16D00DFE40131334668A86D17958E.description: recognize that the visual arts have a history and a variety of cultural purposes and meanings;

DDF11480DFE40131334568A86D17958E.description: Students will understand the visual arts in relation to history and cultures.

DDEEE260DFE40131333E68A86D17958E.description: select and use subject matter, symbols and ideas to communicate meaning.

DDEE9C00DFE40131333D68A86D17958E.description: discuss a variety of sources for art content; and

DDEE55B0DFE40131333C68A86D17958E.description: Students will consider, select and apply a range of subject matter, symbols and ideas.

DDE93410DFE40131332B68A86D17958E.description: use the elements of art and principles of design to communicate ideas.

DDE8ECE0DFE40131332A68A86D17958E.description: describe how different expressive features, and ways of organizing them, cause different responses; and

DDE8A340DFE40131332968A86D17958E.description: identify the different ways visual characteristics are used to convey ideas;

DDE85280DFE40131332868A86D17958E.description: Students will understand and apply elements and organizational principles of art.

DDF75750DFE40131335868A86D17958E.description: read whole, half, dotted half, quarter and eighth notes and rests in 2/4, 3/4, and 4/4 meter signatures;

DDF6FB10DFE40131335768A86D17958E.description: Students will read and notate music.

DDF3B510DFE40131334D68A86D17958E.description: use a variety of sound sources when composing.

DDF03B30DFE40131334268A86D17958E.description: observe two dances and discuss how they are similar and different in terms of one of the elements of dance (such as space) by observing body shapes, levels, pathways; and

DDEFED20DFE40131334168A86D17958E.description: explore, discover and realize multiple solutions to a given movement problem, choose their favorite solution and discuss the reasons for their choice;

DDEF9920DFE40131334068A86D17958E.description: Students will apply analytical and evaluative thinking skills in dance.

DDEC8F10DFE40131333668A86D17958E.description: present their own dances to peers and discuss their meanings with confidence.

document.title: Connecticut Core Standards for Mathematics

D66589C0DFE4013124C668A86D17958E.description: Compare two fractions with the same numerator or the same denominator by reasoning about their size. Recognize that comparisons are valid only when the two fractions refer to the same whole. Record the results of comparisons with the symbols >, =, or <, and justify the conclusions, e.g., by using a visual fraction model.

comments: Example: express 3 in the form 3 = 3/1; recognize that 6/1 = 6.
Example: locate 4/4 and 1 at the same point of a number line diagram.
D66542A0DFE4013124C568A86D17958E.description: Express whole numbers as fractions, and recognize fractions that are equivalent to whole numbers.

D664F270DFE4013124C468A86D17958E.description: Recognize and generate simple equivalent fractions, e.g., 1/2 = 2/4, 4/6 = 2/3). Explain why the fractions are equivalent, e.g., by using a visual fraction model.

D664A860DFE4013124C368A86D17958E.description: Understand two fractions as equivalent (equal) if they are the same size, or the same point on a number line.

D66456F0DFE4013124C268A86D17958E.description: Explain equivalence of fractions in special cases, and compare fractions by reasoning about their size.

D663FF80DFE4013124C168A86D17958E.description: Represent a fraction a/b on a number line diagram by marking off a lengths 1/b from 0. Recognize that the resulting interval has size a/b and that its endpoint locates the number a/b on the number line.

D663B7A0DFE4013124C068A86D17958E.description: Represent a fraction 1/b on a number line diagram by defining the interval from 0 to 1 as the whole and partitioning it into b equal parts. Recognize that each part has size 1/b and that the endpoint of the part based at 0 locates the number 1/b on the number line.

D6636670DFE4013124BF68A86D17958E.description: Understand a fraction as a number on the number line; represent fractions on a number line diagram.

D6631AD0DFE4013124BE68A86D17958E.description: Understand a fraction 1/b as the quantity formed by 1 part when a whole is partitioned into b equal parts; understand a fraction a/b as the quantity formed by a parts of size 1/b.

D662D6B0DFE4013124BD68A86D17958E.description: Develop understanding of fractions as numbers.

comments: Grade 3 expectations in this domain are limited to fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 6, and 8.
Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 100
For example, partition a shape into 4 parts with equal area, and describe the area of each part as 1/4 of the area of the shape.
D6624B30DFE4013124BB68A86D17958E.description: Partition shapes into parts with equal areas. Express the area of each part as a unit fraction of the whole.

D661F160DFE4013124BA68A86D17958E.description: Understand that shapes in different categories (e.g., rhombuses, rectangles, and others) may share attributes (e.g., having four sides), and that the shared attributes can define a larger category (e.g., quadrilaterals). Recognize rhombuses, rectangles, and squares as examples of quadrilaterals, and draw examples of quadrilaterals that do not belong to any of these subcategories.

D661A500DFE4013124B968A86D17958E.description: Reason with shapes and their attributes.

D66102E0DFE4013124B768A86D17958E.description: Solve real world and mathematical problems involving perimeters of polygons, including finding the perimeter given the side lengths, finding an unknown side length, and exhibiting rectangles with the same perimeter and different areas or with the same area and different perimeters.

D660BE80DFE4013124B668A86D17958E.description: Geometric measurement: recognize perimeter as an attribute of plane figures and distinguish between linear and area measures.

D6607EA0DFE4013124B568A86D17958E.description: Recognize area as additive. Find areas of rectilinear figures by decomposing them into non-overlapping rectangles and adding the areas of the non-overlapping parts, applying this technique to solve real world problems.

D6603D50DFE4013124B468A86D17958E.description: Use tiling to show in a concrete case that the area of a rectangle with whole-number side lengths a and b + c is the sum of a × b and a × c. Use area models to represent the distributive property in mathematical reasoning.

D65FFAE0DFE4013124B368A86D17958E.description: Multiply side lengths to find areas of rectangles with whole-number side lengths in the context of solving real world and mathematical problems, and represent whole-number products as rectangular areas in mathematical reasoning.

D65FB530DFE4013124B268A86D17958E.description: Find the area of a rectangle with whole-number side lengths by tiling it, and show that the area is the same as would be found by multiplying the side lengths.

D65F6A00DFE4013124B168A86D17958E.description: Relate area to the operations of multiplication and addition.

D65F2650DFE4013124B068A86D17958E.description: Measure areas by counting unit squares (square cm, square m, square in, square ft, and improvised units).

D65ED4C0DFE4013124AF68A86D17958E.description: A plane figure which can be covered without gaps or overlaps by n unit squares is said to have an area of n square units.

D65E8C40DFE4013124AE68A86D17958E.description: A square with side length 1 unit, called "a unit square," is said to have "one square unit" of area, and can be used to measure area.

D65E4850DFE4013124AD68A86D17958E.description: Recognize area as an attribute of plane figures and understand concepts of area measurement.

D65E0140DFE4013124AC68A86D17958E.description: Geometric measurement: understand concepts of area and relate area to multiplication and to addition.

D65CDFC0DFE4013124A868A86D17958E.description: Generate measurement data by measuring lengths using rulers marked with halves and fourths of an inch. Show the data by making a line plot, where the horizontal scale is marked off in appropriate units— whole numbers, halves, or quarters.

D65C8470DFE4013124A768A86D17958E.description: Draw a scaled picture graph and a scaled bar graph to represent a data set with several categories. Solve one- and two-step "how many more" and "how many less" problems using information presented in scaled bar graphs.
comments: For example, draw a bar graph in which each square in the bar graph might represent 5 pets.

D65DAC60DFE4013124AB68A86D17958E.description: Measure and estimate liquid volumes and masses of objects using standard units of grams (g), kilograms (kg), and liters (l). Add, subtract, multiply, or divide to solve one-step word problems involving masses or volumes that are given in the same units, e.g., by using drawings (such as a beaker with a measurement scale) to represent the problem.
comments: Excludes multiplicative comparison problems (problems involving notions of "times as much";
Excludes compound units such as cm³ and finding the geometric volume of a container.

D65D6C30DFE4013124AA68A86D17958E.description: Tell and write time to the nearest minute and measure time intervals in minutes. Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of time intervals in minutes, e.g., by representing the problem on a number line diagram.

D65D2860DFE4013124A968A86D17958E.description: Solve problems involving measurement and estimation of intervals of time, liquid volumes, and masses of objects.

D65B8C30DFE4013124A468A86D17958E.description: Multiply one-digit whole numbers by multiples of 10 in the range 10—90 (e.g., 9 × 80, 5 × 60) using strategies based on place value and properties of operations.

D65B4C70DFE4013124A368A86D17958E.description: Fluently add and subtract within 1000 using strategies and algorithms based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction.

D65B0C10DFE4013124A268A86D17958E.description: Use place value understanding to round whole numbers to the nearest 10 or 100.

comments: A range of algorithms may be used.
D65AC940DFE4013124A168A86D17958E.description: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to perform multi-digit arithmetic.

D65A7B40DFE4013124A068A86D17958E.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten
comments: Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to whole numbers less than or equal to 1,000,000.

D65A2AC0DFE40131249F68A86D17958E.description: Identify arithmetic patterns (including patterns in the addition table or multiplication table), and explain them using properties of operations.
comments: For example, observe that 4 times a number is always even, and explain why 4 times a number can be decomposed into two equal addends.

D659E400DFE40131249E68A86D17958E.description: Solve two-step word problems using the four operations. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding.
comments: This standard is limited to problems posed with whole numbers and having whole-number answers; students should know how to perform operations in the conventional order when there are no parentheses to specify a particular order (Order of Operations).

D6599EC0DFE40131249D68A86D17958E.description: Solve problems involving the four operations, and identify and explain patterns in arithmetic.

D65954D0DFE40131249C68A86D17958E.description: Fluently multiply and divide within 100, using strategies such as the relationship between multiplication and division (e.g., knowing that 8 × 5 = 40, one knows 40 ÷ 5 = 8) or properties of operations. By the end of Grade 3, know from memory all products of two one-digit numbers.

D6588F80DFE40131249A68A86D17958E.description: Understand division as an unknown-factor problem.
comments: For example, find 32 ÷ 8 by finding the number that makes 32 when multiplied by 8.

D6584C70DFE40131249968A86D17958E.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide.
comments: Students need not use formal terms for these properties.
Example: Knowing that 8 × 5 = 40 and 8 × 2 = 16, one can find 8 × 7 as 8 × (5 + 2) = (8 × 5) + (8 × 2) = 40 + 16 = 56. (Distributive property.)

Example: If 6 × 4 = 24 is known, then 4 × 6 = 24 is also known (Commutative property of multiplication.) 3 × 5 × 2 can be found by 3 × 5 = 15, then 15 × 2 = 30, or by 5 × 2 = 10, then 3 × 10 = 30. (Associative property of multiplication.)

D6580B70DFE40131249868A86D17958E.description: Understand properties of multiplication and the relationship between multiplication and division.

D657C680DFE40131249768A86D17958E.description: Determine the unknown whole number in a multiplication or division equation relating three whole numbers.
comments: For example, determine the unknown number that makes the equation true in each of the equations 8 × ? = 48, 5 = ÷ 3, 6 × 6 = ?.

D65781D0DFE40131249668A86D17958E.description: Use multiplication and division within 100 to solve word problems in situations involving equal groups, arrays, and measurement quantities, e.g., by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

D6573C80DFE40131249568A86D17958E.description: Interpret whole-number quotients of whole numbers, e.g., interpret 56 ÷ 8 as the number of objects in each share when 56 objects are partitioned equally into 8 shares, or as a number of shares when 56 objects are partitioned into equal shares of 8 objects each.
comments: For example, describe a context in which a number of shares or a number of groups can be expressed as 56 ÷ 8.

D656F780DFE40131249468A86D17958E.description: Interpret products of whole numbers, e.g., interpret 5 × 7 as the total number of objects in 5 groups of 7 objects each.
comments: For example, describe a context in which a total number of objects can be expressed as 5 × 7.

D656AB90DFE40131249368A86D17958E.description: Represent and solve problems involving multiplication and division.

comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.
D6561EF0DFE40131249168A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.

D655D210DFE40131249068A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.
D6548F80DFE40131248C68A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

comments: Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

D653E3C0DFE40131248A68A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: Connecticut Core Standards for Mathematics

D68B49A0DFE40131250668A86D17958E.description: Compare two decimals to hundredths by reasoning about their size. Recognize that comparisons are valid only when the two decimals refer to the same whole. Record the results of comparisons with the symbols >, =, or <, and justify the conclusions, e.g., by using a visual model.

D68B04D0DFE40131250568A86D17958E.description: Use decimal notation for fractions with denominators 10 or 100.
comments: For example, rewrite 0.62 as 62/100; describe a length as 0.62 meters; locate 0.62 on a number line diagram.

D68ABAF0DFE40131250468A86D17958E.description: Express a fraction with denominator 10 as an equivalent fraction with denominator 100, and use this technique to add two fractions with respective denominators 10 and 100.
comments: Students who can generate equivalent fractions can develop strategies for adding fractions with unlike denominators in general. But addition and subtraction with unlike denominators in general is not a requirement at this grade.
For example, express 3/10 as 30/100, and add 3/10 + 4/100 = 34/100.

D68A6AE0DFE40131250368A86D17958E.description: Understand decimal notation for fractions, and compare decimal fractions.

comments: For example, if each person at a party will eat 3/8 of a pound of roast beef, and there will be 5 people at the party, how many pounds of roast beef will be needed? Between what two whole numbers does your answer lie?
D68A13A0DFE40131250268A86D17958E.description: Solve word problems involving multiplication of a fraction by a whole number, e.g., by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem.

comments: For example, use a visual fraction model to express 3 × (2/5) as 6 × (1/5), recognizing this product as 6/5. (In general, n × (a/b) = (n × a)/b.)
D689B4B0DFE40131250168A86D17958E.description: Understand a multiple of a/b as a multiple of 1/b, and use this understanding to multiply a fraction by a whole number.

D6896940DFE40131250068A86D17958E.description: Understand a fraction a/b as a multiple of 1/b.
comments: For example, use a visual fraction model to represent 5/4 as the product 5 × (1/4), recording the conclusion by the equation 5/4 = 5 × (1/4).

D6891C40DFE4013124FF68A86D17958E.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication to multiply a fraction by a whole number.

D688D960DFE4013124FE68A86D17958E.description: Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole and having like denominators, e.g., by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem.

D6888950DFE4013124FD68A86D17958E.description: Add and subtract mixed numbers with like denominators, e.g., by replacing each mixed number with an equivalent fraction, and/or by using properties of operations and the relationship between addition and subtraction.

D6883A00DFE4013124FC68A86D17958E.description: Decompose a fraction into a sum of fractions with the same denominator in more than one way, recording each decomposition by an equation. Justify decompositions, e.g., by using a visual fraction model.

D687EC50DFE4013124FB68A86D17958E.description: Understand addition and subtraction of fractions as joining and separating parts referring to the same whole.

D687A5D0DFE4013124FA68A86D17958E.description: Understand a fraction a/b with a > 1 as a sum of fractions 1/b.

D6873F70DFE4013124F968A86D17958E.description: Build fractions from unit fractions by applying and extending previous understandings of operations on whole numbers.

D686F2B0DFE4013124F868A86D17958E.description: Compare two fractions with different numerators and different denominators, e.g., by creating common denominators or numerators, or by comparing to a benchmark fraction such as 1/2. Recognize that comparisons are valid only when the two fractions refer to the same whole. Record the results of comparisons with symbols >, =, or <, and justify the conclusions, e.g., by using a visual fraction model.

D686A3D0DFE4013124F768A86D17958E.description: Explain why a fraction a/b is equivalent to a fraction (n × a)/(n × b) by using visual fraction models, with attention to how the number and size of the parts differ even though the two fractions themselves are the same size. Use this principle to recognize and generate equivalent fractions.

D6865DC0DFE4013124F668A86D17958E.description: Extend understanding of fraction equivalence and ordering.

comments: Grade 3 expectations in this domain are limited to fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 6, and 8.
Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 100

D685D4B0DFE4013124F468A86D17958E.description: Recognize a line of symmetry for a two-dimensional figure as a line across the figure such that the figure can be folded along the line into matching parts. Identify line-symmetric figures and draw lines of symmetry.

D6858DC0DFE4013124F368A86D17958E.description: Classify two-dimensional figures based on the presence or absence of parallel or perpendicular lines, or the presence or absence of angles of a specified size. Recognize right triangles as a category, and identify right triangles.

D68538F0DFE4013124F268A86D17958E.description: Draw points, lines, line segments, rays, angles (right, acute, obtuse), and perpendicular and parallel lines. Identify these in two-dimensional figures.

D684E510DFE4013124F168A86D17958E.description: Draw and identify lines and angles, and classify shapes by properties of their lines and angles.

D68452F0DFE4013124EF68A86D17958E.description: Recognize angle measure as additive. When an angle is decomposed into non-overlapping parts, the angle measure of the whole is the sum of the angle measures of the parts. Solve addition and subtraction problems to find unknown angles on a diagram in real world and mathematical problems, e.g., by using an equation with a symbol for the unknown angle measure.

D6840A20DFE4013124EE68A86D17958E.description: Measure angles in whole-number degrees using a protractor. Sketch angles of specified measure.

D683B800DFE4013124ED68A86D17958E.description: An angle that turns through n one-degree angles is said to have an angle measure of n degrees.

D6835F80DFE4013124EC68A86D17958E.description: An angle is measured with reference to a circle with its center at the common endpoint of the rays, by considering the fraction of the circular arc between the points where the two rays intersect the circle. An angle that turns through 1/360 of a circle is called a "one-degree angle," and can be used to measure angles.

D6831570DFE4013124EB68A86D17958E.description: Recognize angles as geometric shapes that are formed wherever two rays share a common endpoint, and understand concepts of angle measurement:

D682D540DFE4013124EA68A86D17958E.description: Geometric measurement: understand concepts of angle and measure angles.

D6816860DFE4013124E568A86D17958E.description: Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8). Solve problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions by using information presented in line plots.
comments: For example, from a line plot find and interpret the difference in length between the longest and shortest specimens in an insect collection.

D6829080DFE4013124E968A86D17958E.description: Apply the area and perimeter formulas for rectangles in real world and mathematical problems.
comments: For example, find the width of a rectangular room given the area of the flooring and the length, by viewing the area formula as a multiplication equation with an unknown factor.

D6824870DFE4013124E868A86D17958E.description: Use the four operations to solve word problems involving distances, intervals of time, liquid volumes, masses of objects, and money, including problems involving simple fractions or decimals, and problems that require expressing measurements given in a larger unit in terms of a smaller unit. Represent measurement quantities using diagrams such as number line diagrams that feature a measurement scale.

D681FE00DFE4013124E768A86D17958E.description: Know relative sizes of measurement units within one system of units including km, m, cm; kg, g; lb, oz.; l, ml; hr, min, sec. Within a single system of measurement, express measurements in a larger unit in terms of a smaller unit. Record measurement equivalents in a two column table.
comments: For example, know that 1 ft is 12 times as long as 1 in. Express the length of a 4 ft snake as 48 in. Generate a conversion table for feet and inches listing the number pairs (1, 12), (2, 24), (3, 36), …

D681B570DFE4013124E668A86D17958E.description: Solve problems involving measurement and conversion of measurements from a larger unit to a smaller unit.

D67F5360DFE4013124DE68A86D17958E.description: Find whole-number quotients and remainders with up to four-digit dividends and one-digit divisors, using strategies based on place value, the properties of operations, and/or the relationship between multiplication and division. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.

D67F0BB0DFE4013124DD68A86D17958E.description: Multiply a whole number of up to four digits by a one-digit whole number, and multiply two two-digit numbers, using strategies based on place value and the properties of operations. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.

D67EC690DFE4013124DC68A86D17958E.description: Fluently add and subtract multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm.

D67E7DF0DFE4013124DB68A86D17958E.description: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to perform multi-digit arithmetic.

D6809BE0DFE4013124E268A86D17958E.description: Use place value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place.

D6804860DFE4013124E168A86D17958E.description: Read and write multi-digit whole numbers using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form. Compare two multi-digit numbers based on meanings of the digits in each place, using >, =, and < symbols to record the results of comparisons.

comments: For example, recognize that 700 ÷ 70 = 10 by applying concepts of place value and division.
D67FF390DFE4013124E068A86D17958E.description: Recognize that in a multi-digit whole number, a digit in one place represents ten times what it represents in the place to its right.

D67F9750DFE4013124DF68A86D17958E.description: Generalize place value understanding for multi-digit whole numbers.

D67E1DC0DFE4013124DA68A86D17958E.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten
comments: Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to whole numbers less than or equal to 1,000,000.

For example, given the rule "Add 3" and the starting number 1, generate terms in the resulting sequence and observe that the terms appear to alternate between odd and even numbers. Explain informally why the numbers will continue to alternate in this way.
D67DB080DFE4013124D968A86D17958E.description: Generate a number or shape pattern that follows a given rule. Identify apparent features of the pattern that were not explicit in the rule itself.

D67D2880DFE4013124D768A86D17958E.description: Find all factor pairs for a whole number in the range 1—100. Recognize that a whole number is a multiple of each of its factors. Determine whether a given whole number in the range 1—100 is a multiple of a given one-digit number. Determine whether a given whole number in the range 1—100 is prime or composite.

D67CE600DFE4013124D668A86D17958E.description: Gain familiarity with factors and multiples.

D67CA1E0DFE4013124D568A86D17958E.description: Solve multistep word problems posed with whole numbers and having whole-number answers using the four operations, including problems in which remainders must be interpreted. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding.

D67C5AE0DFE4013124D468A86D17958E.description: Multiply or divide to solve word problems involving multiplicative comparison, e.g., by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem, distinguishing multiplicative comparison from additive comparison.

D67C0E20DFE4013124D368A86D17958E.description: Interpret a multiplication equation as a comparison, e.g., interpret 35 = 5 × 7 as a statement that 35 is 5 times as many as 7 and 7 times as many as 5. Represent verbal statements of multiplicative comparisons as multiplication equations.

D67BCD30DFE4013124D268A86D17958E.description: Use the four operations with whole numbers to solve problems.
