document.title: Connecticut Core Standards for English Language Arts & Literacy in History/Social Studies, Science, and Technical Subjects

D80EA370DFE4013127C568A86D17958E.description: Use words and phrases acquired through conversations, reading and being read to, and responding to texts.

D80E4B30DFE4013127C468A86D17958E.description: Distinguish shades of meaning among verbs describing the same general action (e.g., walk, march, strut, prance) by acting out the meanings.

D80DF470DFE4013127C368A86D17958E.description: Identify real-life connections between words and their use (e.g., note places at school that are colorful).

D80D92B0DFE4013127C268A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate understanding of frequently occurring verbs and adjectives by relating them to their opposites (antonyms).

D80D38A0DFE4013127C168A86D17958E.description: Sort common objects into categories (e.g., shapes, foods) to gain a sense of the concepts the categories represent.

D80CEF70DFE4013127C068A86D17958E.description: With guidance and support from adults, explore word relationships and nuances in word meanings.

D80CA870DFE4013127BF68A86D17958E.description: Use the most frequently occurring inflections and affixes (e.g., -ed, -s, re-, un-, pre-, -ful, -less) as a clue to the meaning of an unknown word.

D80C60A0DFE4013127BE68A86D17958E.description: Identify new meanings for familiar words and apply them accurately (e.g., knowing duck is a bird and learning the verb to duck).

D80C15E0DFE4013127BD68A86D17958E.description: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases based on kindergarten reading and content.

D80ACAF0DFE4013127B968A86D17958E.description: Spell simple words phonetically, drawing on knowledge of sound-letter relationships.

D80A8270DFE4013127B868A86D17958E.description: Write a letter or letters for most consonant and short-vowel sounds (phonemes).

D809E9A0DFE4013127B668A86D17958E.description: Capitalize the first word in a sentence and the pronoun I.

D8099160DFE4013127B568A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.

D8093E40DFE4013127B468A86D17958E.description: Produce and expand complete sentences in shared language activities.

D808EC00DFE4013127B368A86D17958E.description: Use the most frequently occurring prepositions (e.g., to, from, in, out, on, off, for, of, by, with).

D8089DF0DFE4013127B268A86D17958E.description: Understand and use question words (interrogatives) (e.g., who, what, where, when, why, how).

D80858E0DFE4013127B168A86D17958E.description: Form regular plural nouns orally by adding /s/ or /es/ (e.g., dog, dogs; wish, wishes).

D8081260DFE4013127B068A86D17958E.description: Use frequently occurring nouns and verbs.

D807BD60DFE4013127AF68A86D17958E.description: Print many upper- and lowercase letters.

D8077180DFE4013127AE68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.

D8068C60DFE4013127AB68A86D17958E.description: Acquire and use accurately a range of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases sufficient for reading, writing, speaking, and listening at the college and career readiness level; demonstrate independence in gathering vocabulary knowledge when encountering an unknown term important to comprehension or expression.

D8063580DFE4013127AA68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.

D805D1B0DFE4013127A968A86D17958E.description: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases by using context clues, analyzing meaningful word parts, and consulting general and specialized reference materials, as appropriate.

D8053B60DFE4013127A768A86D17958E.description: Apply knowledge of language to understand how language functions in different contexts, to make effective choices for meaning or style, and to comprehend more fully when reading or listening.

D804AF90DFE4013127A568A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.

D8046320DFE4013127A468A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.

D803CB40DFE4013127A268A86D17958E.description: College and Career Readiness Anchor Standards for Language

D80380F0DFE4013127A168A86D17958E.description: Speak audibly and express thoughts, feelings, and ideas clearly.

D8033B20DFE4013127A068A86D17958E.description: Add drawings or other visual displays to descriptions as desired to provide additional detail.

D802F120DFE40131279F68A86D17958E.description: Describe familiar people, places, things, and events and, with prompting and support, provide additional detail.

D8024C40DFE40131279D68A86D17958E.description: Ask and answer questions in order to seek help, get information, or clarify something that is not understood.

D801FD40DFE40131279C68A86D17958E.description: Confirm understanding of a text read aloud or information presented orally or through other media by asking and answering questions about key details and requesting clarification if something is not understood.

D801A380DFE40131279B68A86D17958E.description: Continue a conversation through multiple exchanges.

D8014EF0DFE40131279A68A86D17958E.description: Follow agreed-upon rules for discussions (e.g., listening to others and taking turns speaking about the topics and texts under discussion).

D800F6E0DFE40131279968A86D17958E.description: Participate in collaborative conversations with diverse partners about kindergarten topics and texts with peers and adults in small and larger groups.

D7FFB770DFE40131279668A86D17958E.description: Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and communicative tasks, demonstrating command of formal English when indicated or appropriate.

D7FF6DF0DFE40131279568A86D17958E.description: Make strategic use of digital media and visual displays of data to express information and enhance understanding of presentations.

D7FF2290DFE40131279468A86D17958E.description: Present information, findings, and supporting evidence such that listeners can follow the line of reasoning and the organization, development, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.

D7FE78E0DFE40131279268A86D17958E.description: Evaluate a speaker's point of view, reasoning, and use of evidence and rhetoric.

D7FE2B10DFE40131279168A86D17958E.description: Integrate and evaluate information presented in diverse media and formats, including visually, quantitatively, and orally.

D7FDD800DFE40131279068A86D17958E.description: Prepare for and participate effectively in a range of conversations and collaborations with diverse partners, building on others' ideas and expressing their own clearly and persuasively.

D7FD3750DFE40131278E68A86D17958E.description: College and Career Readiness Anchor Standards for Speaking and Listening

D7FBF1C0DFE40131278A68A86D17958E.description: With guidance and support from adults, recall information from experiences or gather information from provided sources to answer a question.

D7FBA820DFE40131278968A86D17958E.description: Participate in shared research and writing projects (e.g., explore a number of books by a favorite author and express opinions about them).

D7FB4F20DFE40131278868A86D17958E.description: Research to Build and Present Knowledge

D7FB04D0DFE40131278768A86D17958E.description: With guidance and support from adults, explore a variety of digital tools to produce and publish writing, including in collaboration with peers.

D7FAB2C0DFE40131278668A86D17958E.description: With guidance and support from adults, respond to questions and suggestions from peers and add details to strengthen writing as needed.

D7F992C0DFE40131278368A86D17958E.description: Use a combination of drawing, dictating, and writing to narrate a single event or several loosely linked events, tell about the events in the order in which they occurred, and provide a reaction to what happened.

D7F94BE0DFE40131278268A86D17958E.description: Use a combination of drawing, dictating, and writing to compose informative/explanatory texts in which they name what they are writing about and supply some information about the topic.

D7F902E0DFE40131278168A86D17958E.description: Use a combination of drawing, dictating, and writing to compose opinion pieces in which they tell a reader the topic or the name of the book they are writing about and state an opinion or preference about the topic or book (e.g., My favorite book is…).

D7F81F20DFE40131277E68A86D17958E.description: Write routinely over extended time frames (time for research, reflection, and revision) and shorter time frames (a single sitting or a day or two) for a range of tasks, purposes, and audiences.

D7F76EF0DFE40131277C68A86D17958E.description: Draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research.

D7F71960DFE40131277B68A86D17958E.description: Gather relevant information from multiple print and digital sources, assess the credibility and accuracy of each source, and integrate the information while avoiding plagiarism.

D7F6B260DFE40131277A68A86D17958E.description: Conduct short as well as more sustained research projects based on focused questions, demonstrating understanding of the subject under investigation.

D7F663F0DFE40131277968A86D17958E.description: Research to Build and Present Knowledge

D7F60320DFE40131277868A86D17958E.description: Use technology, including the Internet, to produce and publish writing and to interact and collaborate with others.

D7F5BA40DFE40131277768A86D17958E.description: Develop and strengthen writing as needed by planning, revising, editing, rewriting, or trying a new approach.

D7F57010DFE40131277668A86D17958E.description: Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development, organization, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.

D7F4BEE0DFE40131277468A86D17958E.description: Write narratives to develop real or imagined experiences or events using effective technique, well-chosen details, and well-structured event sequences.

D7F46330DFE40131277368A86D17958E.description: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine and convey complex ideas and information clearly and accurately through the effective selection, organization, and analysis of content.

D7F40AE0DFE40131277268A86D17958E.description: Write arguments to support claims in an analysis of substantive topics or texts, using valid reasoning and relevant and sufficient evidence.

D7F37A70DFE40131277068A86D17958E.description: College and Career Readiness Anchor Standards for Writing

D7F33190DFE40131276F68A86D17958E.description: Read emergent-reader texts with purpose and understanding.

D7F29820DFE40131276D68A86D17958E.description: Distinguish between similarly spelled words by identifying the sounds of the letters that differ.

D7F23740DFE40131276C68A86D17958E.description: Read common high-frequency words by sight (e.g., the, of, to, you, she, my, is, are, do, does).

D7F1DE30DFE40131276B68A86D17958E.description: Associate the long and short sounds with common spellings (graphemes) for the five major vowels.

D7F18580DFE40131276A68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate basic knowledge of one-to-one letter-sound correspondences by producing the primary or many of the most frequent sound for each consonant.

D7F13880DFE40131276968A86D17958E.description: Know and apply grade-level phonics and word analysis skills in decoding words.

D7F0A220DFE40131276768A86D17958E.description: Add or substitute individual sounds (phonemes) in simple, one-syllable words to make new words.

D7F04530DFE40131276668A86D17958E.description: Isolate and pronounce the initial, medial vowel, and final sounds (phonemes) in three-phoneme (consonent-vowel-consonent, or CVC) words. (This does not include CVCs ending with /l/, /r/, or /x/.)

D7EFFBC0DFE40131276568A86D17958E.description: Blend and segment onsets and rimes of single-syllable spoken words.

D7EFAF50DFE40131276468A86D17958E.description: Count, pronounce, blend, and segment syllables in spoken words.

D7EF0A40DFE40131276268A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate understanding of spoken words, syllables, and sounds (phonemes).

D7EE4B70DFE40131276068A86D17958E.description: Recognize and name all upper- and lowercase letters of the alphabet.

D7EE03B0DFE40131275F68A86D17958E.description: Understand that words are separated by spaces in print.

D7EDBB00DFE40131275E68A86D17958E.description: Recognize that spoken words are represented in written language by specific sequences of letters.

D7ED7090DFE40131275D68A86D17958E.description: Follow words from left to right, top to bottom, and page by page.

D7ED25C0DFE40131275C68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate understanding of the organization and basic features of print.

D7EC3600DFE40131275968A86D17958E.description: Actively engage in group reading activities with purpose and understanding.

D7EBEE50DFE40131275868A86D17958E.description: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity

D7EBA3F0DFE40131275768A86D17958E.description: With prompting and support, identify basic similarities in and differences between two texts on the same topic (e.g., in illustrations, descriptions, or procedures).

D7EB5860DFE40131275668A86D17958E.description: With prompting and support, identify the reasons an author gives to support points in a text.

D7EB07B0DFE40131275568A86D17958E.description: With prompting and support, describe the relationship between illustrations and the text in which they appear (e.g., what person, place, thing, or idea in the text an illustration depicts).

D7EA4860DFE40131275368A86D17958E.description: Name the author and illustrator of a text and define the role of each in presenting the ideas or information in a text.

D7E9F290DFE40131275268A86D17958E.description: Identify the front cover, back cover, and title page of a book.

D7E99B80DFE40131275168A86D17958E.description: With prompting and support, ask and answer questions about unknown words in a text.

D7E8DAF0DFE40131274F68A86D17958E.description: With prompting and support, describe the connection between two individuals, events, ideas, or pieces of information in a text.

D7E894A0DFE40131274E68A86D17958E.description: With prompting and support, identify the main topic and retell key details of a text.

D7E84C30DFE40131274D68A86D17958E.description: With prompting and support, ask and answer questions about key details in a text.

D7E762E0DFE40131274A68A86D17958E.description: Actively engage in group reading activities with purpose and understanding.

D7E70550DFE40131274968A86D17958E.description: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity

D7E67170DFE40131274768A86D17958E.description: With prompting and support, compare and contrast the adventures and experiences of characters in familiar stories.

D7E625E0DFE40131274668A86D17958E.description: With prompting and support, describe the relationship between illustrations and the story in which they appear (e.g., what moment in a story an illustration depicts).

D7E57E00DFE40131274468A86D17958E.description: With prompting and support, name the author and illustrator of a story and define the role of each in telling the story.

D7E52110DFE40131274368A86D17958E.description: Recognize common types of texts (e.g., storybooks, poems).

D7E4C850DFE40131274268A86D17958E.description: Ask and answer questions about unknown words in a text.

D7E42D00DFE40131274068A86D17958E.description: With prompting and support, identify characters, settings, and major events in a story.

D7E3C990DFE40131273F68A86D17958E.description: With prompting and support, retell familiar stories, including key details.

D7E36100DFE40131273E68A86D17958E.description: With prompting and support, ask and answer questions about key details in a text.

D7E29760DFE40131273B68A86D17958E.description: Read and comprehend complex literary and informational texts independently and proficiently.

D7E251F0DFE40131273A68A86D17958E.description: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity

D7E207C0DFE40131273968A86D17958E.description: Analyze how two or more texts address similar themes or topics in order to build knowledge or to compare the approaches the authors take.

D7E1B2E0DFE40131273868A86D17958E.description: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, including the validity of the reasoning as well as the relevance and sufficiency of the evidence.

D7E16E90DFE40131273768A86D17958E.description: Integrate and evaluate content presented in diverse media and formats, including visually and quantitatively, as well as in words.
comments: Please see "Research to Build and Present Knowledge" in Writing and "Comprehension and Collaboration" in Speaking and Listening for additional standards relevant to gathering, assessing, and applying information from print and digital sources.

D7E0E9A0DFE40131273568A86D17958E.description: Assess how point of view or purpose shapes the content and style of a text.

D7E0A6A0DFE40131273468A86D17958E.description: Analyze the structure of texts, including how specific sentences, paragraphs, and larger portions of the text (e.g., a section, chapter, scene, or stanza) relate to each other and the whole.

D7E05FC0DFE40131273368A86D17958E.description: Interpret words and phrases as they are used in a text, including determining technical, connotative, and figurative meanings, and analyze how specific word choices shape meaning or tone.

D7DFBC90DFE40131273168A86D17958E.description: Analyze how and why individuals, events, and ideas develop and interact over the course of a text.

D7DF60B0DFE40131273068A86D17958E.description: Determine central ideas or themes of a text and analyze their development; summarize the key supporting details and ideas.

D7DF1200DFE40131272F68A86D17958E.description: Read closely to determine what the text says explicitly and to make logical inferences from it; cite specific textual evidence when writing or speaking to support conclusions drawn from the text.

D7DE6120DFE40131272D68A86D17958E.description: College and Career Readiness Anchor Standards for Reading

document.title: Connecticut Social Studies Curriculum Framework

D40699A0DFE40131206968A86D17958E.description: explain how specialization increases interdependence among producers, consumers and nations and consequently leads to a higher standard of living.

D4064C60DFE40131206868A86D17958E.description: explain why trade encourages specialization; and

D405E750DFE40131206768A86D17958E.description: explain how specialization leads to more efficient use of economic resources and economic growth;

D4059030DFE40131206668A86D17958E.description: Students will demonstrate how the exchange of goods and services by individuals, groups and nations creates economic interdependence and how trade results in change. Educational experiences will assure that students:

D404F610DFE40131206468A86D17958E.description: analyze the impact of government taxing and spending decisions on specific individuals, businesses, organizations and groups.

D404AFC0DFE40131206368A86D17958E.description: describe how, in a market system, government enforces property rights and provides for standardized systems (e.g., weights and measures, and money); and

D4046900DFE40131206268A86D17958E.description: identify governmental activities that affect the local, state, national and international economy;

D40423E0DFE40131206168A86D17958E.description: identify how fundamental characteristics of a market system (e.g., private property, profits and competition, businesses, labor, banks and government) influence decision making;

D403DEE0DFE40131206068A86D17958E.description: describe the relationships among demand, supply and price and their roles in a market system;

D4039410DFE40131205F68A86D17958E.description: explain that all countries' economies reflect a mix of market, command and traditional elements;

D4034100DFE40131205E68A86D17958E.description: explain how different economic systems (traditional, market and command) use different means to produce, distribute and exchange goods and services;

D402FD80DFE40131205D68A86D17958E.description: Students will demonstrate that various economic systems coexist, and that economic decisions are made by individuals and/or governments, influenced by markets, cultural traditions, individuals and governments in the allocation of goods and services. Educational experiences will assure that students:

D4026490DFE40131205B68A86D17958E.description: explain how technological change and innovation improves a society's productivity and economic growth.

D4021640DFE40131205A68A86D17958E.description: explain economic growth as a sustained increase in the production of goods and services, and that Gross Domestic Product is the basic measure of economic output; and

D401B4B0DFE40131205968A86D17958E.description: illustrate how resources can be used in a variety of ways;

D4016590DFE40131205868A86D17958E.description: present historical and current controversies about the use of resources;

D4011DF0DFE40131205768A86D17958E.description: define opportunity and cost, giving examples;

D400D500DFE40131205668A86D17958E.description: explain that households, businesses, governments and societies face scarcity just as individuals do;

D4008210DFE40131205568A86D17958E.description: compare the resources used by various cultures, countries and/or regions throughout the world;

D4002020DFE40131205468A86D17958E.description: Students will demonstrate that because human, natural and capital resources are limited, individuals, households, businesses and governments must make choices. Educational experiences will assure that students:

D3FF7630DFE40131205268A86D17958E.description: identify the ways ecosystems are transformed through physical and human activities, and can predict the consequences of these activities.

D3FF2A90DFE40131205168A86D17958E.description: demonstrate and explain ways that humans depend on, adapt to and alter the physical environment; and

D3FEE780DFE40131205068A86D17958E.description: draw a freehand map from memory of increasing and appropriate complexity to display geographic information and answer geographic questions;

D3FEA310DFE40131204F68A86D17958E.description: describe human and natural characteristics of places and how they shape or place identity;

D3FE4E70DFE40131204E68A86D17958E.description: use maps, globes, models, graphs, charts and databases to analyze distributions and patterns;

D3FE05B0DFE40131204D68A86D17958E.description: compare and contrast differences among maps, globes, photographs, models and satellite images for solving geographic problems;

D3FDBFA0DFE40131204C68A86D17958E.description: make maps, globes, models, charts and geographic databases;

D3FD70B0DFE40131204B68A86D17958E.description: explain the essential features and functions of maps, globes, photographs, geographic models and satellite images;

D3FD0FC0DFE40131204A68A86D17958E.description: Students will use geographic tools and technology to explain the interactions of humans and the larger environment, and the evolving consequences of those interactions. Educational experiences will assure that students:

D3FC3FE0DFE40131204868A86D17958E.description: identify processes that divide Earth's surface into different political and economic units from local to international levels.

D3FBE820DFE40131204768A86D17958E.description: analyze the formation, characteristics and functions of urban, suburban and rural settlements; and

D3FBA300DFE40131204668A86D17958E.description: explain how patterns of international trade change technology, transportation and communication, and affect economic activities and human migration;

D3FB5D00DFE40131204568A86D17958E.description: explain the patterns and characteristics of human migrations at various levels;

D3FB1280DFE40131204468A86D17958E.description: Students will interpret spatial patterns of human migration, economic activities and political units in Connecticut, the nation and the world. Educational experiences will assure that students:

D3FA4BC0DFE40131204268A86D17958E.description: explain local and world patterns of ecosystem distribution.

D3F9FE60DFE40131204168A86D17958E.description: use basic climatic and other physical data to understand how natural processes shape environmental patterns; and

D3F9B4D0DFE40131204068A86D17958E.description: understand and apply how natural processes influence the formation and location of resources;

D3F96C20DFE40131203F68A86D17958E.description: understand how concepts of physical geography can be applied to explain natural processes;

D3F922F0DFE40131203E68A86D17958E.description: Students will use spatial perspective to explain the physical processes that shape the Earth's surface and its ecosystems. Educational experiences will assure that students:

D41EA6C0DFE4013120B768A86D17958E.description: demonstrate how personal knowledge and experiences influence an individual's perception of places.

D41E4BF0DFE4013120B668A86D17958E.description: locate natural and cultural features in their own and nearby communities, in the United States and in other regions of the world, as needed, to answer geographic questions; and

D41DD0D0DFE4013120B568A86D17958E.description: use latitude and longitude to locate places and calculate differences between places;

D41D8770DFE4013120B468A86D17958E.description: explain and assess how culture affects perception of places and regions;

D41D40F0DFE4013120B368A86D17958E.description: identify and evaluate various perspectives associated with places and regions;

D41CEC00DFE4013120B268A86D17958E.description: examine ways in which regions are interconnected;

D41C7B30DFE4013120B168A86D17958E.description: describe the process and impact of regional change;

D41C2AB0DFE4013120B068A86D17958E.description: describe human and natural characteristics of places and how they shape or place identity;

D41BE450DFE4013120AF68A86D17958E.description: Students will use spatial perspective to identify and analyze the significance of physical and cultural characteristics of places and world regions. Educational experiences will assure that students:

D41B5770DFE4013120AD68A86D17958E.description: describe how domestic groups and organizations seek to influence foreign policy decisions.

D41B0BD0DFE4013120AC68A86D17958E.description: describe how foreign policy decisions may affect domestic groups and organizations; and

D41AB1F0DFE4013120AB68A86D17958E.description: describe the roles of the three branches of U. S. government in developing and conducting foreign policy;

D41A68A0DFE4013120AA68A86D17958E.description: evaluate the impact of significant international events on the United States and on other nations;

D41A2120DFE4013120A968A86D17958E.description: describe the influence of U. S. political, economic and cultural ideas on other nations and the influence of other nations' ideas on the United States;

D419D0A0DFE4013120A868A86D17958E.description: explain what foreign policy is and give examples of United States foreign policy;

D41951A0DFE4013120A768A86D17958E.description: describe the organization of the world into nation-states and describe some ways that nation-states interact with one another;

D418FC70DFE4013120A668A86D17958E.description: Students will demonstrate an understanding of how the major elements of international relations and world affairs affect their lives and the security and well-being of their community, state and nation. Educational experiences will assure that students:

D4185940DFE4013120A468A86D17958E.description: describe the role of the U.S. Constitution in the limitation of government powers.

D41811F0DFE4013120A368A86D17958E.description: compare and evaluate forms of government found outside the United States; and

D417CA00DFE4013120A268A86D17958E.description: explain the meaning of civic life, politics and government;

D4177DE0DFE4013120A168A86D17958E.description: describe and compare unlimited and limited government;

D4171520DFE4013120A068A86D17958E.description: Students will explain that political systems emanate from the need of humans for order, leading to compromise and the establishment of authority. Educational experiences will assure that students:

D4166B10DFE40131209E68A86D17958E.description: identify and apply criteria useful in selecting political leaders at the local, state and national levels.

D4162450DFE40131209D68A86D17958E.description: research an issue of interest and be able to take and defend a position on that issue; and

D415E030DFE40131209C68A86D17958E.description: identify significant characteristics of an effective citizen and know how to influence public policy by participating in the government of their school;

D4159B20DFE40131209B68A86D17958E.description: evaluate situations involving conflicts between rights and propose solutions to these conflicts;

D4154FB0DFE40131209A68A86D17958E.description: explain the meaning of political rights (e.g., right to vote, right to assemble) as distinguished from personal rights (e.g., freedom of speech, freedom of movement);

D4150050DFE40131209968A86D17958E.description: describe how one becomes a citizen of the United States;

D414B8C0DFE40131209868A86D17958E.description: Students will demonstrate knowledge of the rights and responsibilities of citizens to participate in and shape public policy, and contribute to the maintenance of our democratic way of life. Educational experiences will assure that students:

D4141B70DFE40131209668A86D17958E.description: describe how the public agenda is shaped by political leaders and parties, interest groups, the media, public opinion, state and federal courts, and individual citizens.

D413C630DFE40131209568A86D17958E.description: describe means of conflict management, including negotiation, mediation, arbitration and litigation; and

D4137930DFE40131209468A86D17958E.description: explain how an individual's rights to life, liberty and property are protected by the Constitution and criminal and civil laws;

D4132580DFE40131209368A86D17958E.description: understand the process of how a bill becomes a law;

D412DEE0DFE40131209268A86D17958E.description: identify their representatives in national and state legislatures, and the heads of the executive branch at the national, state and local levels;

D41298E0DFE40131209168A86D17958E.description: explain how and why powers are distributed among the national, state and local governments;

D4125040DFE40131209068A86D17958E.description: explain how the Constitution divides the power of government among the executive, legislative and judicial branches, and how each branch can check the power of another;

D41202E0DFE40131208F68A86D17958E.description: demonstrate an understanding of the historical background of the Declaration of Independence;

D411A7C0DFE40131208E68A86D17958E.description: Students will apply knowledge of the U. S. Constitution, how the U. S. system of government works and how the rule of law and the values of liberty and equality have an impact on individual, local, state and national decisions. Educational experiences will assure that students:

D410E810DFE40131208C68A86D17958E.description: be active learners at cultural institutions such as museums and historical exhibitions;

D410A570DFE40131208B68A86D17958E.description: describe and analyze, using historical data and understandings, the options which are available to parties involved in contemporary conflicts or decision making;

D41061B0DFE40131208A68A86D17958E.description: initiate questions and hypotheses about historic events being studied;

D4101600DFE40131208968A86D17958E.description: display empathy for people who have lived in the past; and

D40FC3C0DFE40131208868A86D17958E.description: Students will recognize the continuing importance of historical thinking and historical knowledge in their own lives and in the world in which they live. Educational experiences will assure that students:

D40F3140DFE40131208668A86D17958E.description: describe, explain and analyze the impact of the exchange of ideas on societies, politics, religion, etc.

D40ED2C0DFE40131208568A86D17958E.description: explain how economic factors influenced historical events in the United States and other regions of the world; and

D40E82E0DFE40131208468A86D17958E.description: explain the significance of the achievements of selected individual scientists and inventors from around the world and from various periods;

D40E3CA0DFE40131208368A86D17958E.description: identify and analyze the various causes and effects of movements of groups of people;

D40DE6C0DFE40131208268A86D17958E.description: explain reasons for conflict and the ways conflicts have been resolved;

D40DA490DFE40131208168A86D17958E.description: describe examples of how societies throughout history have used various forms of visual arts, dance, theater, myths, literature and music to express their beliefs, sense of identity and philosophical ideas;

D40D62A0DFE40131208068A86D17958E.description: describe some of the more common forms of government found in the past, giving examples of societies that have practiced them (e.g., monarchy, oligarchy, clan/tribal, autocracy, dynasty, theocracy, republic, democracy);

67E80B81BCF848D8B3CFA152A7327822.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

F2FECAEAE5994BE59B9AF6E039CE173A.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

84E2CA01E4814AE7AD22090E09B76BFF.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: Connecticut Core Standards for Mathematics

D61A9930DFE40131245368A86D17958E.description: Partition circles and rectangles into two and four equal shares, describe the shares using the words halves, fourths, and quarters, and use the phrases half of, fourth of, and quarter of. Describe the whole as two of, or four of the shares. Understand for these examples that decomposing into more equal shares creates smaller shares.

D61A3600DFE40131245268A86D17958E.description: Compose two-dimensional shapes (rectangles, squares, trapezoids, triangles, half-circles, and quarter-circles) or three-dimensional shapes (cubes, right rectangular prisms, right circular cones, and right circular cylinders) to create a composite shape, and compose new shapes from the composite shape.
comments: Students do not need to learn formal names such as "right rectangular prism."

D619EBB0DFE40131245168A86D17958E.description: Distinguish between defining attributes (e.g., triangles are closed and three-sided) versus non-defining attributes (e.g., color, orientation, overall size); build and draw shapes to possess defining attributes.

D6199D40DFE40131245068A86D17958E.description: Reason with shapes and their attributes.

D6191CC0DFE40131244E68A86D17958E.description: Organize, represent, and interpret data with up to three categories; ask and answer questions about the total number of data points, how many in each category, and how many more or less are in one category than in another.

D6188980DFE40131244C68A86D17958E.description: Tell and write time in hours and half-hours using analog and digital clocks.

D617CB50DFE40131244A68A86D17958E.description: Express the length of an object as a whole number of length units, by laying multiple copies of a shorter object (the length unit) end to end; understand that the length measurement of an object is the number of same-size length units that span it with no gaps or overlaps.
comments: Limit to contexts where the object being measured is spanned by a whole number of length units with no gaps or overlaps.

D6178E20DFE40131244968A86D17958E.description: Order three objects by length; compare the lengths of two objects indirectly by using a third object.

D6175090DFE40131244868A86D17958E.description: Measure lengths indirectly and by iterating length units.

D616D200DFE40131244668A86D17958E.description: Subtract multiples of 10 in the range 10-90 from multiples of 10 in the range 10-90 (positive or zero differences), using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used.

D6168F50DFE40131244568A86D17958E.description: Given a two-digit number, mentally find 10 more or 10 less than the number, without having to count; explain the reasoning used.

D6163D60DFE40131244468A86D17958E.description: Add within 100, including adding a two-digit number and a one-digit number, and adding a two-digit number and a multiple of 10, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used. Understand that in adding two-digit numbers, one adds tens and tens, ones and ones; and sometimes it is necessary to compose a ten.

D615F850DFE40131244368A86D17958E.description: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to add and subtract.

D615B300DFE40131244268A86D17958E.description: Compare two two-digit numbers based on meanings of the tens and ones digits, recording the results of comparisons with the symbols >, =, and <.

D6156CF0DFE40131244168A86D17958E.description: The numbers 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90 refer to one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine tens (and 0 ones).

D6151DC0DFE40131244068A86D17958E.description: The numbers from 11 to 19 are composed of a ten and one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine ones.

D614CF60DFE40131243F68A86D17958E.description: 10 can be thought of as a bundle of ten ones — called a "ten."

D6147070DFE40131243E68A86D17958E.description: Understand that the two digits of a two-digit number represent amounts of tens and ones. Understand the following as special cases:

D613EF90DFE40131243C68A86D17958E.description: Count to 120, starting at any number less than 120. In this range, read and write numerals and represent a number of objects with a written numeral.

D6136BF0DFE40131243A68A86D17958E.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten
comments: Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to whole numbers less than or equal to 1,000,000.

D61324D0DFE40131243968A86D17958E.description: Determine the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation relating three whole numbers.
comments: For example, determine the unknown number that makes the equation true in each of the equations 8 + ? = 11, 5 = - 3, 6 + 6 = .

D612CFF0DFE40131243868A86D17958E.description: Understand the meaning of the equal sign, and determine if equations involving addition and subtraction are true or false.
comments: For example, which of the following equations are true and which are false? 6 = 6, 7 = 8 - 1, 5 + 2 = 2 + 5, 4 + 1 = 5 + 2.

D61264E0DFE40131243768A86D17958E.description: Work with addition and subtraction equations.

D6122570DFE40131243668A86D17958E.description: Add and subtract within 20, demonstrating fluency for addition and subtraction within 10. Use strategies such as counting on; making ten (e.g., 8 + 6 = 8 + 2 + 4 = 10 + 4 = 14); decomposing a number leading to a ten (e.g., 13 - 4 = 13 - 3 - 1 = 10 - 1 = 9); using the relationship between addition and subtraction (e.g., knowing that 8 + 4 = 12, one knows 12 - 8 = 4); and creating equivalent but easier or known sums (e.g., adding 6 + 7 by creating the known equivalent 6 + 6 + 1 = 12 + 1 = 13).

D611E810DFE40131243568A86D17958E.description: Relate counting to addition and subtraction (e.g., by counting on 2 to add 2).

comments: For example, subtract 10 - 8 by finding the number that makes 10 when added to 8.
D6116740DFE40131243368A86D17958E.description: Understand subtraction as an unknown-addend problem.

D6112720DFE40131243268A86D17958E.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract.
comments: Students need not use formal terms for these properties.
To add 2 + 6 + 4, the second two numbers can be added to make a ten, so 2 + 6 + 4 = 2 + 10 = 12. (Associative property of addition.)
If 8 + 3 = 11 is known, then 3 + 8 = 11 is also known. (Commutative property of addition.)

D610E310DFE40131243168A86D17958E.description: Understand and apply properties of operations and the relationship between addition and subtraction.

D61096E0DFE40131243068A86D17958E.description: Solve word problems that call for addition of three whole numbers whose sum is less than or equal to 20, e.g., by using objects, drawings, and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

D6105620DFE40131242F68A86D17958E.description: Use addition and subtraction within 20 to solve word problems involving situations of adding to, taking from, putting together, taking apart, and comparing, with unknowns in all positions, e.g., by using objects, drawings, and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

D61016C0DFE40131242E68A86D17958E.description: Represent and solve problems involving addition and subtraction.

comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.
D60F8D70DFE40131242C68A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.

D60F4460DFE40131242B68A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

D60DFD00DFE40131242768A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

D60D62D0DFE40131242568A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: Connecticut Core Standards for Mathematics

D74542E0DFE40131261068A86D17958E.description: Describe qualitatively the functional relationship between two quantities by analyzing a graph (e.g., where the function is increasing or decreasing, linear or nonlinear). Sketch a graph that exhibits the qualitative features of a function that has been described verbally.

D744E770DFE40131260F68A86D17958E.description: Construct a function to model a linear relationship between two quantities. Determine the rate of change and initial value of the function from a description of a relationship or from two (x, y) values, including reading these from a table or from a graph. Interpret the rate of change and initial value of a linear function in terms of the situation it models, and in terms of its graph or a table of values.

D7449B20DFE40131260E68A86D17958E.description: Use functions to model relationships between quantities.

comments: For example, the function A = s² giving the area of a square as a function of its side length is not linear because its graph contains the points (1,1), (2,4) and (3,9), which are not on a straight line.
D7444410DFE40131260D68A86D17958E.description: Interpret the equation y = mx + b as defining a linear function, whose graph is a straight line; give examples of functions that are not linear.

D743E2D0DFE40131260C68A86D17958E.description: Compare properties of two functions each represented in a different way (algebraically, graphically, numerically in tables, or by verbal descriptions).
comments: For example, given a linear function represented by a table of values and a linear function represented by an algebraic expression, determine which function has the greater rate of change.

D7438090DFE40131260B68A86D17958E.description: Understand that a function is a rule that assigns to each input exactly one output. The graph of a function is the set of ordered pairs consisting of an input and the corresponding output.
comments: Function notation is not required in Grade 8.

For example, collect data from students in your class on whether or not they have a curfew on school nights and whether or not they have assigned chores at home. Is there evidence that those who have a curfew also tend to have chores?
D7429970DFE40131260868A86D17958E.description: Understand that patterns of association can also be seen in bivariate categorical data by displaying frequencies and relative frequencies in a two-way table. Construct and interpret a two-way table summarizing data on two categorical variables collected from the same subjects. Use relative frequencies calculated for rows or columns to describe possible association between the two variables.

D7425330DFE40131260768A86D17958E.description: Use the equation of a linear model to solve problems in the context of bivariate measurement data, interpreting the slope and intercept.
comments: For example, in a linear model for a biology experiment, interpret a slope of 1.5 cm/hr as meaning that an additional hour of sunlight each day is associated with an additional 1.5 cm in mature plant height.

D7420C70DFE40131260668A86D17958E.description: Know that straight lines are widely used to model relationships between two quantitative variables. For scatter plots that suggest a linear association, informally fit a straight line, and informally assess the model fit by judging the closeness of the data points to the line.

D741C530DFE40131260568A86D17958E.description: Construct and interpret scatter plots for bivariate measurement data to investigate patterns of association between two quantities. Describe patterns such as clustering, outliers, positive or negative association, linear association, and nonlinear association.

D7417A80DFE40131260468A86D17958E.description: Investigate patterns of association in bivariate data.

D740F5B0DFE40131260268A86D17958E.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems leading to two linear equations in two variables.
comments: For example, given coordinates for two pairs of points, determine whether the line through the first pair of points intersects the line through the second pair.
For example, 3x + 2y = 5 and 3x + 2y = 6 have no solution because 3x + 2y cannot simultaneously be 5 and 6.
D740B320DFE40131260168A86D17958E.description: Solve systems of two linear equations in two variables algebraically, and estimate solutions by graphing the equations. Solve simple cases by inspection.

D7407160DFE40131260068A86D17958E.description: Understand that solutions to a system of two linear equations in two variables correspond to points of intersection of their graphs, because points of intersection satisfy both equations simultaneously.

D7402DA0DFE4013125FF68A86D17958E.description: Analyze and solve pairs of simultaneous linear equations.

D73FE3A0DFE4013125FE68A86D17958E.description: Solve linear equations with rational number coefficients, including equations whose solutions require expanding expressions using the distributive property and collecting like terms.

D73F8850DFE4013125FD68A86D17958E.description: Give examples of linear equations in one variable with one solution, infinitely many solutions, or no solutions. Show which of these possibilities is the case by successively transforming the given equation into simpler forms, until an equivalent equation of the form x = a, a = a, or a = b results (where a and b are different numbers).

D73F2A90DFE4013125FC68A86D17958E.description: Solve linear equations in one variable.

D73EDAF0DFE4013125FB68A86D17958E.description: Analyze and solve linear equations and pairs of simultaneous linear equations.

D73E9070DFE4013125FA68A86D17958E.description: Use similar triangles to explain why the slope m is the same between any two distinct points on a non-vertical line in the coordinate plane; derive the equation y = mx for a line through the origin and the equation y = mx + b for a line intercepting the vertical axis at b.

D73E38A0DFE4013125F968A86D17958E.description: Graph proportional relationships, interpreting the unit rate as the slope of the graph. Compare two different proportional relationships represented in different ways.
comments: For example, compare a distance-time graph to a distance-time equation to determine which of two moving objects has greater speed.

D73DEA30DFE4013125F868A86D17958E.description: Understand the connections between proportional relationships, lines, and linear equations.

D73DA880DFE4013125F768A86D17958E.description: Perform operations with numbers expressed in scientific notation, including problems where both decimal and scientific notation are used. Use scientific notation and choose units of appropriate size for measurements of very large or very small quantities (e.g., use millimeters per year for seafloor spreading). Interpret scientific notation that has been generated by technology.

D73D6670DFE4013125F668A86D17958E.description: Use numbers expressed in the form of a single digit times an integer power of 10 to estimate very large or very small quantities, and to express how many times as much one is than the other.
comments: For example, estimate the population of the United States as 3 × 10<sup>8</sup> and the population of the world as 7 × 10<sup>9</sup>, and determine that the world population is more than 20 times larger.

D73D2490DFE4013125F568A86D17958E.description: Use square root and cube root symbols to represent solutions to equations of the form x² = p and x³ = p, where p is a positive rational number. Evaluate square roots of small perfect squares and cube roots of small perfect cubes. Know that √2 is irrational.

comments: For example, 3² × 3<sup>-5</sup> = 3<sup>-3</sup> = 1/3³ = 1/27.
D73CE150DFE4013125F468A86D17958E.description: Know and apply the properties of integer exponents to generate equivalent numerical expressions.

D73C9990DFE4013125F368A86D17958E.description: Work with radicals and integer exponents.

comments: For example, by truncating the decimal expansion of √2, show that √2 is between 1 and 2, then between 1.4 and 1.5, and explain how to continue on to get better approximations.
D73BF4D0DFE4013125F168A86D17958E.description: Use rational approximations of irrational numbers to compare the size of irrational numbers, locate them approximately on a number line diagram, and estimate the value of expressions (e.g., π²).

D73BB110DFE4013125F068A86D17958E.description: Know that numbers that are not rational are called irrational. Understand informally that every number has a decimal expansion; for rational numbers show that the decimal expansion repeats eventually, and convert a decimal expansion which repeats eventually into a rational number.

D73B6A70DFE4013125EF68A86D17958E.description: Know that there are numbers that are not rational, and approximate them by rational numbers.

D73AE0C0DFE4013125ED68A86D17958E.description: Know the formulas for the volumes of cones, cylinders, and spheres and use them to solve real-world and mathematical problems.

D73A9470DFE4013125EC68A86D17958E.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving volume of cylinders, cones, and spheres.

D73A3730DFE4013125EB68A86D17958E.description: Apply the Pythagorean Theorem to find the distance between two points in a coordinate system.

D739EA00DFE4013125EA68A86D17958E.description: Apply the Pythagorean Theorem to determine unknown side lengths in right triangles in real-world and mathematical problems in two and three dimensions.

D7399EE0DFE4013125E968A86D17958E.description: Explain a proof of the Pythagorean Theorem and its converse.

D7395DA0DFE4013125E868A86D17958E.description: Understand and apply the Pythagorean Theorem.

D7391580DFE4013125E768A86D17958E.description: Use informal arguments to establish facts about the angle sum and exterior angle of triangles, about the angles created when parallel lines are cut by a transversal, and the angle-angle criterion for similarity of triangles.
comments: For example, arrange three copies of the same triangle so that the sum of the three angles appears to form a line, and give an argument in terms of transversals why this is so.

D738AEB0DFE4013125E668A86D17958E.description: Understand that a two-dimensional figure is similar to another if the second can be obtained from the first by a sequence of rotations, reflections, translations, and dilations; given two similar two-dimensional figures, describe a sequence that exhibits the similarity between them.

D7384FF0DFE4013125E568A86D17958E.description: Describe the effect of dilations, translations, rotations, and reflections on two-dimensional figures using coordinates.

comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.
D735D640DFE4013125DD68A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.

D7358490DFE4013125DC68A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

D7342C20DFE4013125D868A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

D7339110DFE4013125D668A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: Connecticut Core Standards for Mathematics

D7C3E6D0DFE40131272B68A86D17958E.description: (+) Analyze decisions and strategies using probability concepts (e.g., product testing, medical testing, pulling a hockey goalie at the end of a game).

D7C33C20DFE40131272968A86D17958E.description: Evaluate and compare strategies on the basis of expected values.
comments: For example, compare a high-deductible versus a low-deductible automobile insurance policy using various, but reasonable, chances of having a minor or a major accident.

D7C2C440DFE40131272868A86D17958E.description: Find the expected payoff for a game of chance.
comments: For example, find the expected winnings from a state lottery ticket or a game at a fast-food restaurant.

D7C256E0DFE40131272768A86D17958E.description: (+) Weigh the possible outcomes of a decision by assigning probabilities to payoff values and finding expected values.
