D63FEF40DFE40131248768A86D17958E.description: Partition circles and rectangles into two, three, or four equal shares, describe the shares using the words halves, thirds, half of, a third of, etc., and describe the whole as two halves, three thirds, four fourths. Recognize that equal shares of identical wholes need not have the same shape.

D63FB1B0DFE40131248668A86D17958E.description: Partition a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares and count to find the total number of them.

D63F7160DFE40131248568A86D17958E.description: Recognize and draw shapes having specified attributes, such as a given number of angles or a given number of equal faces. Identify triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons, and cubes.
comments: Sizes are compared directly or visually, not compared by measuring.

D63F3050DFE40131248468A86D17958E.description: Reason with shapes and their attributes.

D63B3EF0DFE40131247668A86D17958E.description: Draw a picture graph and a bar graph (with single-unit scale) to represent a data set with up to four categories. Solve simple put-together, take-apart, and compare problems using information presented in a bar graph.

D63B81B0DFE40131247768A86D17958E.description: Generate measurement data by measuring lengths of several objects to the nearest whole unit, or by making repeated measurements of the same object. Show the measurements by making a line plot, where the horizontal scale is marked off in whole-number units.

D63EAF90DFE40131248268A86D17958E.description: Solve word problems involving dollar bills, quarters, dimes, nickels, and pennies, using $ and ¢ symbols appropriately.
comments: Example: If you have 2 dimes and 3 pennies, how many cents do you have?

D63E69C0DFE40131248168A86D17958E.description: Tell and write time from analog and digital clocks to the nearest five minutes, using a.m. and p.m.

D63DCC40DFE40131247F68A86D17958E.description: Represent whole numbers as lengths from 0 on a number line diagram with equally spaced points corresponding to the numbers 0, 1, 2, …, and represent whole-number sums and differences within 100 on a number line diagram.

D63D80E0DFE40131247E68A86D17958E.description: Use addition and subtraction within 100 to solve word problems involving lengths that are given in the same units, e.g., by using drawings (such as drawings of rulers) and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

D63D3640DFE40131247D68A86D17958E.description: Relate addition and subtraction to length.

D63CEA00DFE40131247C68A86D17958E.description: Measure to determine how much longer one object is than another, expressing the length difference in terms of a standard length unit.

D63C8C10DFE40131247B68A86D17958E.description: Estimate lengths using units of inches, feet, centimeters, and meters.

D63C4700DFE40131247A68A86D17958E.description: Measure the length of an object twice, using length units of different lengths for the two measurements; describe how the two measurements relate to the size of the unit chosen.

D63C04B0DFE40131247968A86D17958E.description: Measure the length of an object by selecting and using appropriate tools such as rulers, yardsticks, meter sticks, and measuring tapes.

D63BC3E0DFE40131247868A86D17958E.description: Measure and estimate lengths in standard units.

D63A7500DFE40131247368A86D17958E.description: Explain why addition and subtraction strategies work, using place value and the properties of operations.
comments: Explanations may be supported by drawings or objects.

D63A3820DFE40131247268A86D17958E.description: Mentally add 10 or 100 to a given number 100—900, and mentally subtract 10 or 100 from a given number 100—900.

D639FA50DFE40131247168A86D17958E.description: Add and subtract within 1000, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method. Understand that in adding or subtracting three-digit numbers, one adds or subtracts hundreds and hundreds, tens and tens, ones and ones; and sometimes it is necessary to compose or decompose tens or hundreds.

D639BCD0DFE40131247068A86D17958E.description: Add up to four two-digit numbers using strategies based on place value and properties of operations.

D6397CB0DFE40131246F68A86D17958E.description: Fluently add and subtract within 100 using strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction.

D6393360DFE40131246E68A86D17958E.description: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to add and subtract.

D638E6E0DFE40131246D68A86D17958E.description: Compare two three-digit numbers based on meanings of the hundreds, tens, and ones digits, using >, =, and < symbols to record the results of comparisons.

D638A870DFE40131246C68A86D17958E.description: Read and write numbers to 1000 using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form.

D6382240DFE40131246A68A86D17958E.description: The numbers 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800, 900 refer to one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine hundreds (and 0 tens and 0 ones).

D637D230DFE40131246968A86D17958E.description: 100 can be thought of as a bundle of ten tens — called a "hundred."

D63763F0DFE40131246868A86D17958E.description: Understand that the three digits of a three-digit number represent amounts of hundreds, tens, and ones; e.g., 706 equals 7 hundreds, 0 tens, and 6 ones. Understand the following as special cases:

D6313AC0DFE40131246668A86D17958E.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten
comments: Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to whole numbers less than or equal to 1,000,000.

D630FC90DFE40131246568A86D17958E.description: Use addition to find the total number of objects arranged in rectangular arrays with up to 5 rows and up to 5 columns; write an equation to express the total as a sum of equal addends.

D630BBA0DFE40131246468A86D17958E.description: Determine whether a group of objects (up to 20) has an odd or even number of members, e.g., by pairing objects or counting them by 2s; write an equation to express an even number as a sum of two equal addends.

D6307CC0DFE40131246368A86D17958E.description: Work with equal groups of objects to gain foundations for multiplication.

D6303A60DFE40131246268A86D17958E.description: Fluently add and subtract within 20 using mental strategies. By end of Grade 2, know from memory all sums of two one-digit numbers.
comments: See standard 1.OA.6 for a list of mental strategies.

D62FAA90DFE40131246068A86D17958E.description: Use addition and subtraction within 100 to solve one- and two-step word problems involving situations of adding to, taking from, putting together, taking apart, and comparing, with unknowns in all positions, e.g., by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

D62F6B40DFE40131245F68A86D17958E.description: Represent and solve problems involving addition and subtraction.

D62EDE70DFE40131245D68A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

D62E86E0DFE40131245C68A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

D62D3680DFE40131245868A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

D62C93D0DFE40131245668A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: Connecticut Arts Curriculum Framework

DEA1F220DFE4013134C368A86D17958E.description: apply visual arts skills and understandings to solve problems relevant to a variety of careers.

DEA18CF0DFE4013134C268A86D17958E.description: create and solve interdisciplinary problems using multimedia; and

DEA141A0DFE4013134C168A86D17958E.description: compare the creative processes used in the visual arts with the creative processes used in the other arts and non-arts disciplines;

DEA0F6C0DFE4013134C068A86D17958E.description: analyze and compare characteristics of the visual arts within a particular historical period or style with ideas, issues or themes of that period or style;

DEA0AAA0DFE4013134BF68A86D17958E.description: Students will make connections between the visual arts, other disciplines and daily life.

DE9E5870DFE4013134B868A86D17958E.description: apply critical and aesthetic criteria (e.g., technique, formal and expressive qualities, content) in order to improve their own works of art.

DE9E08C0DFE4013134B768A86D17958E.description: defend personal interpretations using reasoned argument; and

DE9DBDD0DFE4013134B668A86D17958E.description: reflect critically on various interpretations to better understand specific works of art;

DE9D7320DFE4013134B568A86D17958E.description: research and analyze historic meaning and purpose in varied works of art;

DE9D2250DFE4013134B468A86D17958E.description: Students will reflect upon, describe, analyze, interpret and evaluate their own and others' work.

DE9289B0DFE40131349368A86D17958E.description: compare works of art to one another in terms of history, aesthetics and culture; justify conclusions made and use these conclusions to inform their own art making.

DE9232D0DFE40131349268A86D17958E.description: analyze common characteristics of visual arts evident across time and among cultural/ethnic groups in order to formulate analyses, evaluations and interpretations of meaning; and

DE91DA10DFE40131349168A86D17958E.description: analyze and interpret art works in terms of form, cultural and historical context, and purpose;

DE9184E0DFE40131349068A86D17958E.description: Students will understand the visual arts in relation to history and cultures.

DE8CDDF0DFE40131348168A86D17958E.description: use subject matter, symbols, ideas and themes that demonstrate knowledge of contexts, and cultural and aesthetic values to communicate intended meaning.

DE8C8DF0DFE40131348068A86D17958E.description: use, record and develop ideas for content over time; and

DE8C2D90DFE40131347F68A86D17958E.description: Students will consider, select and apply a range of subject matter, symbols and ideas.

DE89EAF0DFE40131347868A86D17958E.description: apply comprehension and skill in incorporating the elements of art and principles of design to generate multiple solutions to and effectively solvea variety of visual art problems.

DE899E90DFE40131347768A86D17958E.description: judge the effectiveness of different ways of using visual characteristics in conveying ideas; and

DE895400DFE40131347668A86D17958E.description: Students will understand and apply elements and organizational principles of art.

DE803AF0DFE40131345D68A86D17958E.description: communicate ideas consistently at a high level of effectiveness in at least one visual arts medium.

DE7FCF90DFE40131345C68A86D17958E.description: conceive and create original works of art that demonstrate a connection between personal expression and the intentional use of art materials, techniques and processes; and

DE7F61A0DFE40131345B68A86D17958E.description: apply media, techniques and processes with sufficient skill, confidence and sensitivity that their intentions are understood;

DE7F17E0DFE40131345A68A86D17958E.description: Students will understand, select and apply media, techniques and processes.

DEACEBE0DFE4013134E568A86D17958E.description: analyze the effect of their own cultural experiences on their dramatic work.

DEAC9DB0DFE4013134E468A86D17958E.description: identify cultural and historical sources of American theatre and musical theatre; and

DEAC4780DFE4013134E368A86D17958E.description: identify and compare the lives, works and influence of representative theatre artists in various cultures and historical periods;

DEABFF20DFE4013134E268A86D17958E.description: compare similar themes in drama from various cultures and historical periods, create informal and formal performances using these themes, and discuss how theatre can reveal universal concepts;

DEABB240DFE4013134E168A86D17958E.description: Students will demonstrate an understanding of context by analyzing and comparing theatre in various cultures and historical periods.

DEAB1D70DFE4013134DF68A86D17958E.description: constructively evaluate their own and others' collaborative efforts in informal and formal productions.

DEAABDF0DFE4013134DE68A86D17958E.description: analyze and critique performances and constructively suggest alternative artistic choices; and

DEAA60A0DFE4013134DD68A86D17958E.description: articulate and justify personal aesthetic criteria for critiquing dramatic texts and events by comparing artistic intent with the final performance;

DEAA1010DFE4013134DC68A86D17958E.description: construct social meanings from informal and formal productions from a variety of cultures and historical periods, and relate these to current personal, national and international issues;

DEA9BD50DFE4013134DB68A86D17958E.description: Students will analyze, critique and construct meanings from works of theatre.

DEA61B80DFE4013134D068A86D17958E.description: explore career opportunities in theatre and theatre-related fields.

DEA5D420DFE4013134CF68A86D17958E.description: create and solve interdisciplinary problems using theatre; and

DEA58B00DFE4013134CE68A86D17958E.description: illustrate the integration of arts media in informal or formal presentations;

DEA533D0DFE4013134CD68A86D17958E.description: determine how the nondramatic art forms are modified to enhance the expression of ideas and emotions in theatre;

DEA4EAA0DFE4013134CC68A86D17958E.description: describe and compare the materials, elements and means of communicating in theatre, dance, music and the visual arts;

DEA495F0DFE4013134CB68A86D17958E.description: Students will make connections between theatre, other disciplines and daily life.

DE98E480DFE4013134A768A86D17958E.description: identify and research cultural, historical and symbolic clues in dramatic texts, and evaluate the validity and practicality of the information to help make artistic choices for informal and formal productions.

DE988BB0DFE4013134A668A86D17958E.description: Students will research, evaluate and apply cultural and historical information to make artistic choices.

DE965120DFE40131349F68A86D17958E.description: effectively communicate directorial choices toa small ensemble for improvised or scripted scenes.

DE9607C0DFE40131349E68A86D17958E.description: justify selection of text, interpretation and visual/aural choices; and

DE95BDD0DFE40131349D68A86D17958E.description: develop multiple interpretations and visual and aural production choices for scripts and production ideas and choose those that are most appropriate;

DE957280DFE40131349C68A86D17958E.description: Students will direct by planning or interpreting works of theatre and by organizing and conducting rehearsals.

DE90EA30DFE40131348E68A86D17958E.description: design coherent stage management, promotional and business practices.

DE90A2B0DFE40131348D68A86D17958E.description: apply technical skills and understandings, including scientific and technological advances, to collaboratively and safely create functional scenery, properties, lighting, sound, costumes and makeup; and

DE905B30DFE40131348C68A86D17958E.description: develop designs that use visual and aural elements to convey environments that clearly support the text;

DE901240DFE40131348B68A86D17958E.description: analyze a variety of dramatic texts from cultural and historical perspectives to determine production requirements;

DE8FB9F0DFE40131348A68A86D17958E.description: explain the physical and chemical properties of the technical aspects of theatre, such as light, color, electricity, paint and makeup;

DE8F6E10DFE40131348968A86D17958E.description: Students will design and produce the technical elements of theatre through artistic interpretation and execution.

DE8359E0DFE40131346768A86D17958E.description: in an ensemble, create and sustain characters.

DE82F930DFE40131346668A86D17958E.description: compare and demonstrate acting techniques and methods from a variety of periods and styles; and

DE82A1A0DFE40131346568A86D17958E.description: analyze the physical, emotional and social dimensions of characters found in dramatic texts from various genres and media;

DE825790DFE40131346468A86D17958E.description: Students will act by developing, communicating and sustaining characters.

DE7E7B40DFE40131345868A86D17958E.description: construct imaginative scripts and collaborate with actors to refine scripts so that story and meaning are conveyed to an audience.

DE7E2FA0DFE40131345768A86D17958E.description: Students will create theatre through improvising, writing and refining scripts.

DEB0AE40DFE4013134F068A86D17958E.description: identify various roles musicians perform, cite representative individuals who have functioned in each role, and describe their activities and performances.

DEB05FF0DFE4013134EF68A86D17958E.description: identify sources of American music genres, trace the evolution of those genres, and cite well-known musicians associated with them; and

DEB005D0DFE4013134EE68A86D17958E.description: classify by genre or style and by historical period or culture unfamiliar but representative aural examples of music, and explain the reasoning behind their classifications;

DEAFB980DFE4013134ED68A86D17958E.description: Students will understand music in relation to history and culture.

DEAF1CC0DFE4013134EB68A86D17958E.description: apply music skills and understandings to solve problems relevant to a variety of careers.

DEAEC570DFE4013134EA68A86D17958E.description: explain ways in which the principles and subject matter of music and various disciplines outside the arts are interrelated; and

DEAE6DD0DFE4013134E968A86D17958E.description: compare characteristics of two or more arts within a particular historical period or style and cite examples from various cultures;

DEAE10D0DFE4013134E868A86D17958E.description: explain how elements, artistic processes and organizational principles are used in similar and distinctive ways in the various arts, and cite examples;

DEADBE20DFE4013134E768A86D17958E.description: Students will make connections between music, other disciplines and daily life.

DEA905B0DFE4013134D968A86D17958E.description: evaluate a performance, composition, arrangement or improvisation by comparing it to similar or exemplary models.

DEA8A820DFE4013134D868A86D17958E.description: evolve specific criteria for making informed, critical evaluations of the quality and effectiveness of performances, compositions, arrangements and improvisations and apply the criteria in their personal participation in music; and

DEA85A50DFE4013134D768A86D17958E.description: Students will evaluate music and music performances.

DEA00C90DFE4013134BD68A86D17958E.description: identify and explain compositional devices and techniques used to provide unity and variety and tension and release in a musical work, and give examples of other works that make similar uses of these devices and techniques.

DE9FB2C0DFE4013134BC68A86D17958E.description: demonstrate extensive knowledge of the technical vocabulary of music; and

DE9F5B10DFE4013134BB68A86D17958E.description: analyze aural examples of a varied repertoire of music representing diverse genres and cultures by describing the uses of music elements and expressive devices;

DE9F0750DFE4013134BA68A86D17958E.description: Students will listen to, describe and analyze music.

DE9A3600DFE4013134AB68A86D17958E.description: sight-read, accurately and expressively, music with a difficulty level of 3, on a scale of 1 to 6.

DE99DC50DFE4013134AA68A86D17958E.description: demonstrate the ability to read an instrumental or vocal score of up to four staves by describing how the elements of music are used; and

DE997FA0DFE4013134A968A86D17958E.description: Students will read and notate music.

DE97F660DFE4013134A468A86D17958E.description: compose and arrange music for voices and various acoustic and electronic instruments, demonstrating knowledge of the ranges and traditional use of the sound sources.

DE97A970DFE4013134A368A86D17958E.description: arrange pieces for voices or instruments other than those for which the pieces were written in ways that preserve or enhance the expressive effect of the music; and

DE975A30DFE4013134A268A86D17958E.description: compose music in several distinct styles, demonstrating creativity in using the elements of music for expressive effect;

DE96FA20DFE4013134A168A86D17958E.description: Students will compose and arrange music.

DE8B8780DFE40131347D68A86D17958E.description: improvise original melodies over given chord progressions, each in a consistent style, meter and tonality.

DE8B3140DFE40131347C68A86D17958E.description: improvise rhythmic and melodic variations on given pentatonic melodies and melodies in major and minor keys; and

DE8A9400DFE40131347A68A86D17958E.description: Students will improvise melodies, variations and accompaniments.

DE88B190DFE40131347468A86D17958E.description: perform in small ensembles with one student on a part.

DE884790DFE40131347368A86D17958E.description: perform an appropriate part in an ensemble, demonstrating well-developed ensemble skills; and

DE87CF30DFE40131347268A86D17958E.description: perform with expression and technical accuracy a large and varied repertoire of instrumental literature with a difficulty level of 4, on a scale of 1 to 6

DE8780B0DFE40131347168A86D17958E.description: Students will play, alone and with others, a varied repertoire of instrumental music.

DE816B10DFE40131346168A86D17958E.description: sing ensemble music for up to four parts, with and without accompaniment; and

DE811B90DFE40131346068A86D17958E.description: sing with expression and technical accuracy a large and varied repertoire of vocal literature with a difficulty level of 4, on a scale of 1 to 6, including some songs performed from memory;

DE80D350DFE40131345F68A86D17958E.description: Students will sing, alone and with others, a varied repertoire of songs.

DEA7ADC0DFE4013134D568A86D17958E.description: create an interdisciplinary project using media technologies (such as video, computer) that presents dance in a new or enhanced form (such as video dance, video/computer-aided live performance, or animation).

DEA743E0DFE4013134D468A86D17958E.description: identify commonalties and differences between dance and other disciplines with regard to fundamental concepts such as materials, elements and ways of communicating meaning; and

DEA6F160DFE4013134D368A86D17958E.description: create an interdisciplinary project based on a theme identified by the student, including dance and two other disciplines;

DEA6A880DFE4013134D268A86D17958E.description: Students will make connections between dance, other disciplines and daily life.

DEA3EC70DFE4013134C968A86D17958E.description: effectively communicate how lifestyle choices affect the dancer.

DEA396B0DFE4013134C868A86D17958E.description: analyze historical and cultural images of the body in dance and compare these to images of the body in contemporary media; and

DEA33B20DFE4013134C768A86D17958E.description: create and demonstrate movement sequences which stretch and strengthen the main muscle groups;

DEA2F0B0DFE4013134C668A86D17958E.description: reflect upon their own progress and personal growth during their study of dance;

DEA2A480DFE4013134C568A86D17958E.description: Students will make connections between dance and healthful living.

DE9C6540DFE4013134B268A86D17958E.description: create and answer questions about dance and dancers prior to the 20th century.

DE9C1AA0DFE4013134B168A86D17958E.description: analyze historical and cultural images of the body in dance and compare these to contemporary images; and

DE9BCC60DFE4013134B068A86D17958E.description: create a time line illustrating important dance events in the 20th century;

DE9B8110DFE4013134AF68A86D17958E.description: perform and describe similarities and differences between two contemporary theatrical forms of dance or two folk dance forms;

DE9B3880DFE4013134AE68A86D17958E.description: perform or discuss the traditions and technique of a classical dance form;

DE9AEE00DFE4013134AD68A86D17958E.description: Students will demonstrate an understanding of dance in various cultures and historical periods.

DE94CC30DFE40131349A68A86D17958E.description: formulate and answer their own aesthetic questions (such as: What is it that makes a particular dance that dance? What makes a successful dance successful?).

DE947F30DFE40131349968A86D17958E.description: analyze the style of a choreographer or cultural form, then create a dance study in that style and evaluate the results in discussion with peers; and

DE943060DFE40131349868A86D17958E.description: compare the work of two contrasting choreographers using a given set of artistic criteria;

DE93DB00DFE40131349768A86D17958E.description: establish a set of artistic criteria and apply it in evaluating their own work and that of others;

DE9381D0DFE40131349668A86D17958E.description: create a dance and revise it over time, articulating the reasons for their artistic decisions and what was lost and gained by those decisions;

DE9333D0DFE40131349568A86D17958E.description: Students will apply analytical and evaluative thinking skills in dance.

DE8ED300DFE40131348768A86D17958E.description: create a dance that effectively communicates a contemporary social theme or a topic of personal significance.

DE8E8320DFE40131348668A86D17958E.description: compare and contrast how meaning is communicated in two of their own dances; and

DE8E2EF0DFE40131348568A86D17958E.description: examine the ways in which a dance creates and conveys meaning by considering the dance from different cultural perspectives;

DE8DD9C0DFE40131348468A86D17958E.description: formulate and answer questions about how movement choices communicate abstract ideas in dance;

DE8D83E0DFE40131348368A86D17958E.description: Students will understand how dance creates and communicates meaning.

DE86C520DFE40131346F68A86D17958E.description: describe how a choreographer manipulated and developed the basic movement content in a dance.

DE865BB0DFE40131346E68A86D17958E.description: develop an idea independently from initial inception through to presentation for an audience; and

DE85F420DFE40131346D68A86D17958E.description: choreograph duets and small-group dances demonstrating an understanding of choreographic principles, processes and structures both in collaborative groups and as choreographer/director;

DE857C30DFE40131346C68A86D17958E.description: demonstrate understanding of structures or forms (such as theme and variation, rondo, round, structured improvisation and chance) through brief dance studies;

DE8501A0DFE40131346B68A86D17958E.description: choreograph dances which effectively demonstrate a range of choreographic principles;

DE8477D0DFE40131346A68A86D17958E.description: use effectively a range of choreographic processes;

DE840E70DFE40131346968A86D17958E.description: Students will understand choreographic principles, processes and structures.

DE7D7A60DFE40131345568A86D17958E.description: describe the characteristics of a particular choreographer's movement vocabulary.

DE7D1BC0DFE40131345468A86D17958E.description: memorize and perform a varied repertoire of dances; and

DE7CD0D0DFE40131345368A86D17958E.description: perform dances confidently, communicating the artistic intention of the choreographer;

DE7C8480DFE40131345268A86D17958E.description: create and perform combinations and variations in a broad dynamic range;

DE7BCD50DFE40131345068A86D17958E.description: use spatial awareness to heighten artistic expression;

DE7B7210DFE40131344F68A86D17958E.description: identify and perform basic dance steps, positions and patterns for dance from two different styles or traditions, demonstrating clarity and stylistic accuracy;

DE7B13C0DFE40131344E68A86D17958E.description: demonstrate appropriate skeletal alignment, body-part articulation, strength, flexibility, agility and coordination in locomotor and nonlocomotor movements with consistency and reliability;

DE7AC4E0DFE40131344D68A86D17958E.description: Students will identify and perform movement elements and dance skills.

document.title: Connecticut Science Curriculum Grade-Level Expectations

D318D380DFE401311E7668A86D17958E.description: Develop a model or illustration to show the relative positions of the Earth, sun and moon during a lunar and solar eclipse and explain how those positions influence the view from Earth.

D3189740DFE401311E7568A86D17958E.description: Use a model to demonstrate the phases of the moon relative to the position of the sun, Earth and moon.

D3185920DFE401311E7468A86D17958E.description: Conduct and report on an investigation that shows how the Earth's tilt on its axis and position around the sun relates to the intensity of light striking the Earth's surface.

D3181980DFE401311E7368A86D17958E.description: Compare the revolution times of all the planets and relate it to their distance from the sun.

D317C900DFE401311E7268A86D17958E.description: Investigate and report in writing how the Earth's revolution around the sun affects changes in daylight and seasons.

D31785F0DFE401311E7168A86D17958E.description: Distinguish between rotation of Earth on its axis and its elliptical revolution around the sun.

D31740F0DFE401311E7068A86D17958E.description: Describe in writing how gravitational attraction and the inertia of objects in the solar system keep them on a predictable elliptical pathway.

D316FF10DFE401311E6F68A86D17958E.description: Relate the strength of gravitational force between two objects to their mass and the distance between the centers of the two objects and provide examples.

D316C0A0DFE401311E6E68A86D17958E.description: The solar system is composed of planets and other objects that orbit the sun.

D3162E70DFE401311E6C68A86D17958E.description: Illustrate how the circular motion of an object is caused by a center-seeking force (centripetal force) resulting in the object's constant acceleration.

D315EBD0DFE401311E6B68A86D17958E.description: Design and conduct an experiment to determine how gravity and friction (air resistance) affect a falling object.

D315AE40DFE401311E6A68A86D17958E.description: Express mathematically how the mass of an object and the force acting on it affect its acceleration.

D3156F60DFE401311E6968A86D17958E.description: Assess in writing the relationship between an object's mass and its inertia when at rest and in motion.

D3151FD0DFE401311E6868A86D17958E.description: Investigate and demonstrate how unbalanced forces cause acceleration (change in speed and/or direction of an object's motion).

D314D710DFE401311E6768A86D17958E.description: Predict the motion of an object given the magnitude and direction of forces acting on it (net force).

D3147710DFE401311E6668A86D17958E.description: Create and interpret distance-time graphs for objects moving at constant and nonconstant speeds.

D3141B10DFE401311E6568A86D17958E.description: Calculate the average speed of a moving object, and distinguish between instantaneous speed and average speed of an object.

D313DAA0DFE401311E6468A86D17958E.description: Use appropriate tools and techniques to make observations and gather data to determine how forces, including friction, act on an object to change its position over time in relation to a fixed point of reference.

D3139BE0DFE401311E6368A86D17958E.description: An object's inertia causes it to continue moving the way it is moving unless it is acted upon by a force to change its motion.

D3131A00DFE401311E6168A86D17958E.description: Use technology to simulate how engineers plan, test and revise bridge designs given parameters including cost, time, safety and aesthetics.

D312DB30DFE401311E6068A86D17958E.description: Conduct an experiment to discover and report on a bridge's ability to support a load based on the interplay of tension and compression forces that result in a net force of zero.

D3129960DFE401311E5F68A86D17958E.description: Explain in writing the advantages and disadvantages of truss, beam and suspension bridge design and visually identify each bridge.

D3123F00DFE401311E5E68A86D17958E.description: Identify the forces acting on a truss, beam and suspension bridge, including compression, tension and gravity using models, pictures or diagrams.

D31200B0DFE401311E5D68A86D17958E.description:
In the design of structures there is a need to consider factors such as function, materials, safety, cost and appearance.
This content standard is an application of the concepts in content standard 8.1 and should be integrated into the same unit.

D31181E0DFE401311E5B68A86D17958E.description: Describe in writing the role of the germ cells in the formation of the human zygote and its resulting 23 pairs of chromosomes, the 23rd of which determines gender and the other 22 of which determine the characteristics of that offspring.

D3113CA0DFE401311E5A68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate the relationship of corresponding genes on pairs of chromosomes to traits inherited by offspring.

D310F290DFE401311E5968A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast the events and processes that occur when a human egg is fertilized or not fertilized.

D310AB20DFE401311E5868A86D17958E.description: Investigate and report on the role of hormone production as it initiates and regulates the creation of male and female germ cells from birth through adolescence and into adulthood.

D3105600DFE401311E5768A86D17958E.description: Identify the major structures in human male and female reproductive systems and explain where meiosis and gamete formation take place.

D3100CD0DFE401311E5668A86D17958E.description: Illustrate and chart the purpose, cell type (somatic and germ) and resulting chromosome count during cell division in mitosis and meiosis.

D30FB750DFE401311E5568A86D17958E.description: Describe the structure, location and function of chromosomes, genes and DNA and how they relate to each other in the living cell.

D30F6C40DFE401311E5468A86D17958E.description: Relate the continued existence of any species to its successful reproduction and explain in writing the factors that contribute to successful reproduction.

D30F2550DFE401311E5368A86D17958E.description: Reproduction is a characteristic of living systems and it is essential for the continuation of every species.

document.title: Connecticut Science Curriculum Grade-Level Expectations

D2D24970DFE401311DCE68A86D17958E.description: Predict the effect an environmental change, such as drought or forest destruction, might have on the community of living things.

D2D1FFA0DFE401311DCD68A86D17958E.description: Distinguish between naturally occurring changes in ecosystems and those caused by human activity.

D2D1C070DFE401311DCC68A86D17958E.description: Analyze food webs to describe how energy is transferred from plants to various animals in an ecosystem.

D2D15FE0DFE401311DCB68A86D17958E.description: Design and conduct simple investigations to record interactions among producers, consumers, herbivores, carnivores, omnivores and decomposers in an ecosystem.

D2D10D40DFE401311DCA68A86D17958E.description: Draw diagrams showing how the sun's energy enters and is transferred from producers to consumers in a local land or aquatic food chain.

D2D0CC40DFE401311DC968A86D17958E.description: Give examples of ways that living and nonliving things are interdependent within an ecosystem.

D2D07770DFE401311DC868A86D17958E.description: All organisms depend on the living and nonliving features of the environment for survival.

D2CFCCE0DFE401311DC668A86D17958E.description: Predict the effect of an object's mass on its motion.

D2CF8EA0DFE401311DC568A86D17958E.description: Describe how friction forces caused by air resistance or interactions between surface materials affect the motion of objects.

D2CF4E30DFE401311DC468A86D17958E.description: Design and conduct experiments to determine how the motion of objects is related to the mass of the object and the strength of the force applied.

D2CF0810DFE401311DC368A86D17958E.description: Use measurement tools and standard units to compare and contrast the motion of objects such as toy cars, balls, model rockets or planes in terms of change in position, speed and direction.

D2CEAB30DFE401311DC268A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate that a force can cause an object to start moving, stop, or change speed or direction.

D2CE5450DFE401311DC168A86D17958E.description: The position and motion of objects can be changed by pushing or pulling.

D2CDDBA0DFE401311DBF68A86D17958E.description: Give examples of uses of magnets (e.g., motors, generators, household devices).

D2CDA000DFE401311DBE68A86D17958E.description: Investigate how magnets react with other magnets and analyze findings to identify patterns in the interactions between north and south poles of magnets.

D2CD6430DFE401311DBD68A86D17958E.description: Design procedures to move objects and separate mixtures of solids using magnets.

D2CD27D0DFE401311DBC68A86D17958E.description: Describe materials that are attracted by magnets.

D2CCE7B0DFE401311DBB68A86D17958E.description: Observe magnetic effects associated with electricity and investigate factors that affect the strength of an electromagnet.

D2CC9F50DFE401311DBA68A86D17958E.description: Develop a method for testing conductivity, and analyze data to generalize about which materials are good electrical conductors and which are good insulators.

D2CC6210DFE401311DB968A86D17958E.description: Predict whether diagrammed circuit configurations will light a bulb.

D2CC24F0DFE401311DB868A86D17958E.description: Draw labeled diagrams of complete and incomplete circuits and explain necessary components and how components must be arranged to make a complete circuit.

D2CBE810DFE401311DB768A86D17958E.description: Construct complete (closed) and incomplete (open) series circuits in which electrical energy is transformed into heat, light, sound and/or motion energy.

D2CBA880DFE401311DB668A86D17958E.description: Electrical and magnetic energy can be transferred and transformed.

D2CB2000DFE401311DB468A86D17958E.description: Present evidence to support a scientific claim about the relationship between the amount and speed of moving water and the size of earth materials moved (e.g., silt, pebbles, boulders).

D2CAD4D0DFE401311DB368A86D17958E.description: Pose testable questions and employ simple equipment and measuring tools to collect data about factors that affect erosion (e.g., type of earth material in an area, volume of moving water, slope of land, vegetation coverage).

D2CA93C0DFE401311DB268A86D17958E.description: Design and conduct simple investigations to determine how moving water (flowing downhill or in ocean waves) causes changes to the land, the coastline or the course of a stream or river.

D2CA51D0DFE401311DB168A86D17958E.description: Use models to demonstrate that topography causes precipitation landing on earth to move in streams and rivers from higher to lower elevations.

D2CA1020DFE401311DB068A86D17958E.description: Describe the role of the sun's energy (i.e., heating and cooling) in the continuous cycling of water between the earth and the atmosphere through evaporation, condensation and precipitation.

D2C9CBF0DFE401311DAF68A86D17958E.description: Water has a major role in shaping the Earth's surface.

document.title: Connecticut Science Curriculum Grade-Level Expectations

D2F3F9E0DFE401311E1B68A86D17958E.description: Predict what will happen to a population based on current trends (fires, disease, overhunting, development) and defend the prediction.

D2F3BB90DFE401311E1A68A86D17958E.description: Explain the impact of environmental conditions such as climate, elevation, topography or water quality on food chains.

D2F63930DFE401311E2368A86D17958E.description: Distinguish a food chain from a food web and identify local examples of each.

D2F5F5B0DFE401311E2268A86D17958E.description: Create and interpret graphs that illustrate the fluctuation of populations over time.

D2F5B410DFE401311E2168A86D17958E.description: Identify local examples of predator-prey relationships and justify the impact of each type of population on the other.

D2F56BE0DFE401311E2068A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast how energy and matter flow in a Connecticut ecosystem, emphasizing the interactions among producers, consumers and decomposers.

D2F52010DFE401311E1F68A86D17958E.description: Investigate and report on the effects of abiotic factors on a plant's ability to photosynthesize.

D2F4C890DFE401311E1E68A86D17958E.description: Express in general terms how plants and other photosynthetic organisms use the sun's energy.

D2F474F0DFE401311E1D68A86D17958E.description: Defend the statement, "The sun is the main source of energy on Earth."

D2F43740DFE401311E1C68A86D17958E.description: Design and conduct a scientific investigation to explore the porosity and permeability of soils and their ability to support different plant life.

D2F37BF0DFE401311E1968A86D17958E.description: Analyze and interpret how biotic and abiotic factors interact within a given ecosystem.

D2F33AE0DFE401311E1868A86D17958E.description: An ecosystem is composed of all the populations that are living in a certain space and the physical factors with which they interact.

D2F2ACE0DFE401311E1668A86D17958E.description: Debate the effectiveness of a law designed to protect water resources.

D2F26D80DFE401311E1568A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast the general structures, processes and limitations of a septic system to a secondary wastewater treatment plant.

D2F22A20DFE401311E1468A86D17958E.description: Research and evaluate in writing the effects of common point and nonpoint water pollutants in Connecticut.

D2F1E990DFE401311E1368A86D17958E.description: Use appropriate maps to locate and identify the major watersheds that drain into Long Island Sound and analyze how the topography influences the way water moves in the Long Island Sound watershed.

D2F19A10DFE401311E1268A86D17958E.description: Investigate and explain in writing how substances, both harmful and beneficial, dissolve in and are carried by surface and ground water.

D2F13000DFE401311E1168A86D17958E.description: Research the differences in quantities between fresh water (solid and liquid) and salt water covering the Earth's surface and report on the impact to humans.

D2F0DA80DFE401311E1068A86D17958E.description: Observe, analyze and record the unique physical and chemical properties of water.

D2F09D70DFE401311E0F68A86D17958E.description: Discuss and chart the reasons why water is essential for life.

D2F05EC0DFE401311E0E68A86D17958E.description:
Water moving across and through earth materials carries with it the products of human activities.
This content standard is an application of the concepts in content standard 6.3 and should be integrated into the same unit.

D2ED68D0DFE401311E0468A86D17958E.description: Design a weather forecast based on collected weather data.

D2EFDCE0DFE401311E0C68A86D17958E.description: Examine and explain that global winds are caused by uneven heating of the Earth's surface and the rotation of the Earth.

D2EF8220DFE401311E0B68A86D17958E.description: Investigate and explain the movement of local winds, including "sea breezes" and "land breezes," based on the uneven heating of the Earth's surface and a change in air pressure.

D2EF1530DFE401311E0A68A86D17958E.description: Research and give examples of heat transfer and local weather differences in Connecticut.

D2EED1E0DFE401311E0968A86D17958E.description: Design, conduct and report in writing an investigation that reveals different substances absorb and release heat at different rates.

D2EE8D90DFE401311E0868A86D17958E.description: Illustrate the transfer of energy as matter changes phase.

D2EE4B40DFE401311E0768A86D17958E.description: Investigate and report on how the introduction of heat affects the motion of particles and the distance between them.

D2EE0880DFE401311E0668A86D17958E.description: Describe in writing how solar energy drives Earth's weather systems.

D2EDC180DFE401311E0568A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate how changes in temperature, pressure, moisture and density of air affect weather patterns (e.g., air masses and air pressure.)

D2ED16C0DFE401311E0368A86D17958E.description: Compare the composition and structure of the Earth's atmospheric layers.

D2ECCE90DFE401311E0268A86D17958E.description: Variations in the amount of the sun's energy hitting the Earth's surface affect daily and seasonal weather patterns.

D2EC3BC0DFE401311E0068A86D17958E.description: Use the patterns in the Periodic Table to locate metals, semimetals and nonmetals and to predict the general characteristics of an element.

D2EBEC40DFE401311DFF68A86D17958E.description: Conduct and report on an investigation that uses physical means such as particle size, density, solubility and magnetism to separate substances in a mixture.

D2EB9BF0DFE401311DFE68A86D17958E.description: Differentiate between a mixture and an element or compound and identify examples.

D2EB5ED0DFE401311DFD68A86D17958E.description: Illustrate the differences in the physical and chemical properties of a molecule and the individual atoms that bonded to form that molecule.

D2EB2160DFE401311DFC68A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast the properties of a metal (aluminum, iron, etc.) with a nonmetal (oxygen, carbon, etc.)

D2EAE300DFE401311DFB68A86D17958E.description: Explain that density (mass/volume) is a characteristic property that can be used to identify an element or substance.

D2EAA400DFE401311DFA68A86D17958E.description: Describe the structure of the atom and its component parts.

D2EA6190DFE401311DF968A86D17958E.description: Materials can be classified as pure substances or mixtures, depending on their chemical and physical properties.

document.title: Connecticut Core Standards for Mathematics

D6B14390DFE40131254868A86D17958E.description: Solve real world problems involving division of unit fractions by non-zero whole numbers and division of whole numbers by unit fractions, e.g., by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem.
comments: For example, how much chocolate will each person get if 3 people share 1/2 lb of chocolate equally? How many 1/3-cup servings are in 2 cups of raisins?

D6B0F570DFE40131254768A86D17958E.description: Interpret division of a whole number by a unit fraction, and compute such quotients.
comments: For example, create a story context for 4 ÷ (1/5), and use a visual fraction model to show the quotient. Use the relationship between multiplication and division to explain that 4 ÷ (1/5) = 20 because 20 × (1/5) = 4.

D6B0A0D0DFE40131254668A86D17958E.description: Interpret division of a unit fraction by a non-zero whole number, and compute such quotients.
comments: For example, create a story context for (1/3) ÷ 4, and use a visual fraction model to show the quotient. Use the relationship between multiplication and division to explain that (1/3) ÷ 4 = 1/12 because (1/12) × 4 = 1/3.

D6B051A0DFE40131254568A86D17958E.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of division to divide unit fractions by whole numbers and whole numbers by unit fractions.
comments: Students able to multiply fractions in general can develop strategies to divide fractions in general, by reasoning about the relationship between multiplication and division. But division of a fraction by a fraction is not a requirement at this grade

D6B004B0DFE40131254468A86D17958E.description: Solve real world problems involving multiplication of fractions and mixed numbers, e.g., by using visual fraction models or equations to represent the problem.

D6AFC000DFE40131254368A86D17958E.description: Explaining why multiplying a given number by a fraction greater than 1 results in a product greater than the given number (recognizing multiplication by whole numbers greater than 1 as a familiar case); explaining why multiplying a given number by a fraction less than 1 results in a product smaller than the given number; and relating the principle of fraction equivalence a/b = (n×a)/(n×b) to the effect of multiplying a/b by 1.

D6AF6370DFE40131254268A86D17958E.description: Comparing the size of a product to the size of one factor on the basis of the size of the other factor, without performing the indicated multiplication.

D6AEAF20DFE40131254068A86D17958E.description: Find the area of a rectangle with fractional side lengths by tiling it with unit squares of the appropriate unit fraction side lengths, and show that the area is the same as would be found by multiplying the side lengths. Multiply fractional side lengths to find areas of rectangles, and represent fraction products as rectangular areas.

comments: For example, use a visual fraction model to show (2/3) × 4 = 8/3, and create a story context for this equation. Do the same with (2/3) × (4/5) = 8/15. (In general, (a/b) × (c/d) = ac/bd.)
D6AE69F0DFE40131253F68A86D17958E.description: Interpret the product (a/b) × q as a parts of a partition of q into b equal parts; equivalently, as the result of a sequence of operations a × q ÷ b.

D6AE2660DFE40131253E68A86D17958E.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication to multiply a fraction or whole number by a fraction.

D6ADD7D0DFE40131253D68A86D17958E.description: Interpret a fraction as division of the numerator by the denominator (a/b = a ÷ b). Solve word problems involving division of whole numbers leading to answers in the form of fractions or mixed numbers, e.g., by using visual fraction models or equations to represent the problem.
comments: For example, interpret 3/4 as the result of dividing 3 by 4, noting that 3/4 multiplied by 4 equals 3, and that when 3 wholes are shared equally among 4 people each person has a share of size 3/4. If 9 people want to share a 50-pound sack of rice equally by weight, how many pounds of rice should each person get? Between what two whole numbers does your answer lie?

D6AD88F0DFE40131253C68A86D17958E.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication and division to multiply and divide fractions.

D6AD4430DFE40131253B68A86D17958E.description: Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole, including cases of unlike denominators, e.g., by using visual fraction models or equations to represent the problem. Use benchmark fractions and number sense of fractions to estimate mentally and assess the reasonableness of answers.
comments: For example, recognize an incorrect result 2/5 + 1/2 = 3/7, by observing that 3/7 < 1/2.

D6ACFD60DFE40131253A68A86D17958E.description: Add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators (including mixed numbers) by replacing given fractions with equivalent fractions in such a way as to produce an equivalent sum or difference of fractions with like denominators.
comments: For example, 2/3 + 5/4 = 8/12 + 15/12 = 23/12. (In general, a/b + c/d = (ad + bc)/bd.)

D6ACB9E0DFE40131253968A86D17958E.description: Use equivalent fractions as a strategy to add and subtract fractions.

comments: Grade 3 expectations in this domain are limited to fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 6, and 8.
Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 100

D6AC27F0DFE40131253768A86D17958E.description: Classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties.

D6ABD750DFE40131253668A86D17958E.description: Understand that attributes belonging to a category of two-dimensional figures also belong to all subcategories of that category.
comments: For example, all rectangles have four right angles and squares are rectangles, so all squares have four right angles.

D6AB84A0DFE40131253568A86D17958E.description: Classify two-dimensional figures into categories based on their properties.

D6AB37D0DFE40131253468A86D17958E.description: Represent real world and mathematical problems by graphing points in the first quadrant of the coordinate plane, and interpret coordinate values of points in the context of the situation.

D6AAE850DFE40131253368A86D17958E.description: Use a pair of perpendicular number lines, called axes, to define a coordinate system, with the intersection of the lines (the origin) arranged to coincide with the 0 on each line and a given point in the plane located by using an ordered pair of numbers, called its coordinates. Understand that the first number indicates how far to travel from the origin in the direction of one axis, and the second number indicates how far to travel in the direction of the second axis, with the convention that the names of the two axes and the coordinates correspond (e.g., x-axis and x-coordinate, y-axis and y-coordinate).

D6AAA470DFE40131253268A86D17958E.description: Graph points on the coordinate plane to solve real-world and mathematical problems.

D6AA12E0DFE40131253068A86D17958E.description: Recognize volume as additive. Find volumes of solid figures composed of two non-overlapping right rectangular prisms by adding the volumes of the non-overlapping parts, applying this technique to solve real world problems.

D6A9C910DFE40131252F68A86D17958E.description: Apply the formulas V = l × w × h and V = b × h for rectangular prisms to find volumes of right rectangular prisms with whole-number edge lengths in the context of solving real world and mathematical problems.

D6A97DA0DFE40131252E68A86D17958E.description: Find the volume of a right rectangular prism with whole-number side lengths by packing it with unit cubes, and show that the volume is the same as would be found by multiplying the edge lengths, equivalently by multiplying the height by the area of the base. Represent threefold whole-number products as volumes, e.g., to represent the associative property of multiplication.

D6A93780DFE40131252D68A86D17958E.description: Relate volume to the operations of multiplication and addition and solve real world and mathematical problems involving volume.

D6A8F460DFE40131252C68A86D17958E.description: Measure volumes by counting unit cubes, using cubic cm, cubic in, cubic ft, and improvised units.

D6A8AC60DFE40131252B68A86D17958E.description: A solid figure which can be packed without gaps or overlaps using n unit cubes is said to have a volume of n cubic units.

D6A85770DFE40131252A68A86D17958E.description: A cube with side length 1 unit, called a "unit cube," is said to have "one cubic unit" of volume, and can be used to measure volume.

D6A81030DFE40131252968A86D17958E.description: Recognize volume as an attribute of solid figures and understand concepts of volume measurement.

D6A7C200DFE40131252868A86D17958E.description: Geometric measurement: understand concepts of volume and relate volume to multiplication and to addition.

D6A6E790DFE40131252568A86D17958E.description: Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8). Use operations on fractions for this grade to solve problems involving information presented in line plots.
comments: For example, given different measurements of liquid in identical beakers, find the amount of liquid each beaker would contain if the total amount in all the beakers were redistributed equally.

D6A780E0DFE40131252768A86D17958E.description: Convert among different-sized standard measurement units within a given measurement system (e.g., convert 5 cm to 0.05 m), and use these conversions in solving multi-step, real world problems.

D6A73D30DFE40131252668A86D17958E.description: Convert like measurement units within a given measurement system.

D6A5E830DFE40131252268A86D17958E.description: Add, subtract, multiply, and divide decimals to hundredths, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used.

D6A59CD0DFE40131252168A86D17958E.description: Find whole-number quotients of whole numbers with up to four-digit dividends and two-digit divisors, using strategies based on place value, the properties of operations, and/or the relationship between multiplication and division. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.

D6A55480DFE40131252068A86D17958E.description: Fluently multiply multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm.

D6A505A0DFE40131251F68A86D17958E.description: Perform operations with multi-digit whole numbers and with decimals to hundredths.

D6A4C640DFE40131251E68A86D17958E.description: Use place value understanding to round decimals to any place.

D6A485C0DFE40131251D68A86D17958E.description: Compare two decimals to thousandths based on meanings of the digits in each place, using >, =, and < symbols to record the results of comparisons.

D6A44170DFE40131251C68A86D17958E.description: Read and write decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form, e.g., 347.392 = 3 × 100 + 4 × 10 + 7 × 1 + 3 × (1/10) + 9 × (1/100) + 2 × (1/1000).

D6A3F440DFE40131251B68A86D17958E.description: Read, write, and compare decimals to thousandths.

D6A3A4C0DFE40131251A68A86D17958E.description: Explain patterns in the number of zeros of the product when multiplying a number by powers of 10, and explain patterns in the placement of the decimal point when a decimal is multiplied or divided by a power of 10. Use whole-number exponents to denote powers of 10.

D6A34C10DFE40131251968A86D17958E.description: Recognize that in a multi-digit number, a digit in one place represents 10 times as much as it represents in the place to its right and 1/10 of what it represents in the place to its left.

D6A2CF80DFE40131251768A86D17958E.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten
comments: Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to whole numbers less than or equal to 1,000,000.

D6A28E20DFE40131251668A86D17958E.description: Generate two numerical patterns using two given rules. Identify apparent relationships between corresponding terms. Form ordered pairs consisting of corresponding terms from the two patterns, and graph the ordered pairs on a coordinate plane.
comments: For example, given the rule "Add 3" and the starting number 0, and given the rule "Add 6" and the starting number 0, generate terms in the resulting sequences, and observe that the terms in one sequence are twice the corresponding terms in the other sequence. Explain informally why this is so.

For example, express the calculation "add 8 and 7, then multiply by 2" as 2 × (8 + 7). Recognize that 3 × (18932 + 921) is three times as large as 18932 + 921, without having to calculate the indicated sum or product.
D6A20D10DFE40131251468A86D17958E.description: Write simple expressions that record calculations with numbers, and interpret numerical expressions without evaluating them.

D6A1CC20DFE40131251368A86D17958E.description: Use parentheses, brackets, or braces in numerical expressions, and evaluate expressions with these symbols.

D6A0E8B0DFE40131251068A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

D6A097B0DFE40131250F68A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.
D69F4D50DFE40131250B68A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

comments: Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

D69E9090DFE40131250968A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

DA6ACAE0DFE401312C6D68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.

DA6A7B40DFE401312C6C68A86D17958E.description: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases by using context clues, analyzing meaningful word parts, and consulting general and specialized reference materials, as appropriate.
