D8889F30DFE4013128AC68A86D17958E.description: Develop and strengthen writing as needed by planning, revising, editing, rewriting, or trying a new approach.

D88857A0DFE4013128AB68A86D17958E.description: Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development, organization, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.

D887C120DFE4013128A968A86D17958E.description: Write narratives to develop real or imagined experiences or events using effective technique, well-chosen details, and well-structured event sequences.

D8876D90DFE4013128A868A86D17958E.description: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine and convey complex ideas and information clearly and accurately through the effective selection, organization, and analysis of content.

D88715B0DFE4013128A768A86D17958E.description: Write arguments to support claims in an analysis of substantive topics or texts, using valid reasoning and relevant and sufficient evidence.

D8862310DFE4013128A468A86D17958E.description: Use context to confirm or self-correct word recognition and understanding, rereading as necessary.

D885CCA0DFE4013128A368A86D17958E.description: Read on-level text orally with accuracy, appropriate rate, and expression on successive readings.

D88566C0DFE4013128A268A86D17958E.description: Read on-level text with purpose and understanding.

D8851EE0DFE4013128A168A86D17958E.description: Read with sufficient accuracy and fluency to support comprehension.

D88480E0DFE40131289F68A86D17958E.description: Recognize and read grade-appropriate irregularly spelled words.

D8843300DFE40131289E68A86D17958E.description: Identify words with inconsistent but common spelling-sound correspondences.

D883E450DFE40131289D68A86D17958E.description: Decode words with common prefixes and suffixes.

D8839390DFE40131289C68A86D17958E.description: Decode regularly spelled two-syllable words with long vowels.

D88347C0DFE40131289B68A86D17958E.description: Know spelling-sound correspondences for additional common vowel teams.

D8830070DFE40131289A68A86D17958E.description: Distinguish long and short vowels when reading regularly spelled one-syllable words.

D882B880DFE40131289968A86D17958E.description: Know and apply grade-level phonics and word analysis skills in decoding words.

D881C7A0DFE40131289668A86D17958E.description: By the end of year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, in the grades 2—3 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.

D8812030DFE40131289468A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast the most important points presented by two texts on the same topic.

D880C9F0DFE40131289368A86D17958E.description: Describe how reasons support specific points the author makes in a text.

D8805C70DFE40131289268A86D17958E.description: Explain how specific images (e.g., a diagram showing how a machine works) contribute to and clarify a text.

D87FBD20DFE40131289068A86D17958E.description: Identify the main purpose of a text, including what the author wants to answer, explain, or describe.

D87F7200DFE40131288F68A86D17958E.description: Know and use various text features (e.g., captions, bold print, subheadings, glossaries, indexes, electronic menus, icons) to locate key facts or information in a text efficiently.

D87F23A0DFE40131288E68A86D17958E.description: Determine the meaning of words and phrases in a text relevant to a grade 2 topic or subject area.

D87E5B80DFE40131288C68A86D17958E.description: Describe the connection between a series of historical events, scientific ideas or concepts, or steps in technical procedures in a text.

D87E14B0DFE40131288B68A86D17958E.description: Identify the main topic of a multiparagraph text as well as the focus of specific paragraphs within the text.

D87DCD90DFE40131288A68A86D17958E.description: Ask and answer such questions as who, what, where, when, why, and how to demonstrate understanding of key details in a text.

D87CED80DFE40131288768A86D17958E.description: By the end of the year, read and comprehend literature, including stories and poetry, in the grades 2—3 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.

D87BA4F0DFE40131288368A86D17958E.description: Use information gained from the illustrations and words in a print or digital text to demonstrate understanding of its characters, setting, or plot.

D87AEDB0DFE40131288168A86D17958E.description: Acknowledge differences in the points of view of characters, including by speaking in a different voice for each character when reading dialogue aloud.

D87AA3D0DFE40131288068A86D17958E.description: Describe the overall structure of a story, including describing how the beginning introduces the story and the ending concludes the action.

D87A59C0DFE40131287F68A86D17958E.description: Describe how words and phrases (e.g., regular beats, alliteration, rhymes, repeated lines) supply rhythm and meaning in a story, poem, or song.

D879CC20DFE40131287D68A86D17958E.description: Describe how characters in a story respond to major events and challenges.

D87980D0DFE40131287C68A86D17958E.description: Recount stories, including fables and folktales from diverse cultures, and determine their central message, lesson, or moral.

D8790540DFE40131287B68A86D17958E.description: Ask and answer such questions as who, what, where, when, why, and how to demonstrate understanding of key details in a text.

D8781690DFE40131287868A86D17958E.description: Read and comprehend complex literary and informational texts independently and proficiently.

D877CA80DFE40131287768A86D17958E.description: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity

D8777E00DFE40131287668A86D17958E.description: Analyze how two or more texts address similar themes or topics in order to build knowledge or to compare the approaches the authors take.

D8772D90DFE40131287568A86D17958E.description: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, including the validity of the reasoning as well as the relevance and sufficiency of the evidence.

D876E5E0DFE40131287468A86D17958E.description: Integrate and evaluate content presented in diverse media and formats, including visually and quantitatively, as well as in words.

D8760C40DFE40131287168A86D17958E.description: Analyze the structure of texts, including how specific sentences, paragraphs, and larger portions of the text (e.g., a section, chapter, scene, or stanza) relate to each other and the whole.

D875B910DFE40131287068A86D17958E.description: Interpret words and phrases as they are used in a text, including determining technical, connotative, and figurative meanings, and analyze how specific word choices shape meaning or tone.

D87509E0DFE40131286E68A86D17958E.description: Analyze how and why individuals, events, and ideas develop and interact over the course of a text.

D874B670DFE40131286D68A86D17958E.description: Determine central ideas or themes of a text and analyze their development; summarize the key supporting details and ideas.

D8746730DFE40131286C68A86D17958E.description: Read closely to determine what the text says explicitly and to make logical inferences from it; cite specific textual evidence when writing or speaking to support conclusions drawn from the text.

document.title: Connecticut Core Standards for Mathematics

E2A54EC031EC4DBABDBE2CF8E633B361.description: (+) Analyze decisions and strategies using probability concepts (e.g., product testing, medical testing, pulling a hockey goalie at the end of a game).

1AD91E274C7448349BD207751DFDC7B1.description: (+) Use probabilities to make fair decisions (e.g., drawing by lots, using a random number generator).

9646B1BFE5DC4153BD765AC751456A0A.description: Evaluate and compare strategies on the basis of expected values.
comments: For example, compare a high-deductible versus a low-deductible automobile insurance policy using various, but reasonable, chances of having a minor or a major accident.

F66497B64893403EBBCE7B9589BCC59A.description: Find the expected payoff for a game of chance.
comments: For example, find the expected winnings from a state lottery ticket or a game at a fast-food restaurant.

5E8083E450414517B5629706415325BC.description: (+) Weigh the possible outcomes of a decision by assigning probabilities to payoff values and finding expected values.

5E25781B503E406B9CACFB746038BE66.description: Use probability to evaluate outcomes of decisions

22F6777A6A5A410AA804860C401DA2A0.description: (+) Develop a probability distribution for a random variable defined for a sample space in which probabilities are assigned empirically; find the expected value.
comments: For example, find a current data distribution on the number of TV sets per household in the United States, and calculate the expected number of sets per household. How many TV sets would you expect to find in 100 randomly selected households?

255B30B105B64CB882D2BEAFB023AE5F.description: (+) Develop a probability distribution for a random variable defined for a sample space in which theoretical probabilities can be calculated; find the expected value.
comments: For example, find the theoretical probability distribution for the number of correct answers obtained by guessing on all five questions of a multiple-choice test where each question has four choices, and find the expected grade under various grading schemes.

C3D4FCEE8B0D47E2BA1ACD1AD4055C11.description: (+) Calculate the expected value of a random variable; interpret it as the mean of the probability distribution.

22D694F1D15D4EF3A14C01687ADA9166.description: (+) Define a random variable for a quantity of interest by assigning a numerical value to each event in a sample space; graph the corresponding probability distribution using the same graphical displays as for data distributions.

569FA84894EA4133B49A57BEA333DCEF.description: Calculate expected values and use them to solve problems

A7B0049DFA8C40D5A4C435CD4F966D7E.description: (+) Use permutations and combinations to compute probabilities of compound events and solve problems.

D6069EB395594CE5BBB1BC06EFDD0CFA.description: (+) Apply the general Multiplication Rule in a uniform probability model, P(A and B) = P(A)P(B|A) = P(B)P(A|B), and interpret the answer in terms of the model.

36B0965401A34589B01368A52821E222.description: Apply the Addition Rule, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B), and interpret the answer in terms of the model.

DD8FC574FFDD45CA80E531072DBA822A.description: Find the conditional probability of A given B as the fraction of B's outcomes that also belong to A, and interpret the answer in terms of the model.

E555DA3E507B42A8BB3815C95D37E755.description: Use the rules of probability to compute probabilities of compound events in a uniform probability model

comments: For example, compare the chance of having lung cancer if you are a smoker with the chance of being a smoker if you have lung cancer.
8094E415C5FB4C36884AA415963025CC.description: Recognize and explain the concepts of conditional probability and independence in everyday language and everyday situations.

850F75D5960A4CD9AAB44ADC14E6B565.description: Construct and interpret two-way frequency tables of data when two categories are associated with each object being classified. Use the two-way table as a sample space to decide if events are independent and to approximate conditional probabilities.
comments: For example, collect data from a random sample of students in your school on their favorite subject among math, science, and English. Estimate the probability that a randomly selected student from your school will favor science given that the student is in tenth grade. Do the same for other subjects and compare the results.

7AB8563763E146BD98D7AA9D8774A434.description: Understand the conditional probability of A given B as P(A and B)/P(B), and interpret independence of A and B as saying that the conditional probability of A given B is the same as the probability of A, and the conditional probability of B given A is the same as the probability of B.

101E7B7C1B724BC1961AA11377ED6ECA.description: Understand that two events A and B are independent if the probability of A and B occurring together is the product of their probabilities, and use this characterization to determine if they are independent.

033E9B66209143B0AF5B2D0AB3873CE7.description: Describe events as subsets of a sample space (the set of outcomes) using characteristics (or categories) of the outcomes, or as unions, intersections, or complements of other events ("or," "and," "not").

A89D39547B514E37BC474915C6F816CB.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

8B2D0553FF824F4F9DF7F142B604B136.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

A9160935072E481ABFC5E2B84A44E1B3.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

74F39DD82C8F4A27A816318B7A54AA8C.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

674460231CB44B33B9B11ACE4E22057A.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.
1C57F4303B514095B5DDB6887D50E841.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

comments: Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.
2EF5EFFE8CE34010A9240A88FC19A68C.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.

70994095CA184AC39ED27BB5E7EF2D6E.description:
Identify the contributing factors that underlie multiple and varied points of view about school,
community, and civic issues.

B4CB41320A2347FD916A3CE1CBB95CE8.description:
Illustrate how individuals and groups in the Revolutionary Era and today have and can effect
change (e.g., school, community, and state issues).

F36A6AEBBA844B26B3EC0DB1C97D3BF1.description:
Identify how the political beliefs are represented in the Preamble of the United States
Constitution.

4050040DAC61402FB6DFE5F80A31F908.description:
Explain the role of the Constitution in establishing a system of government in the United
States (e.g., federalism, separation of power, states’ rights).

FD0C7D3FC5B04B869706D7A386DB0B2A.description:
Explain how rules were established at the end of the American Revolution by identifying laws
that promoted and limited personal liberties (e.g., citizenship, property, suffrage).

32FED6EBA6B14C5AB709C8AE4C3D9B18.description:
Examine the origins and purpose of key provisions of the United States Constitution (e.g.,
checks and balances, limited government, popular sovereignty, republicanism, separations of
powers, federalism).

991AD70081714A9080F39E09230178C6.description: The United States Constitution and Civic Participation

16A90BAE237A4CED847F07A3DB927D6E.description: Explain the causes and effects of the Treaty of Paris (e.g., economic, political, social).

BDC1BB0500504D069ADB728B8B826E10.description:
Explain economic interdependence between the New England, Middle, and Southern colonies
during the American Revolution (e.g., trade, efforts to support the continental cause).

E90D72B98D5B4E369B2513679D9901B8.description:
Develop a claim about significant people, places or events in Connecticut during the
American Revolution (e.g., Jonathan Occum, Israel Putnam, Hannah Bunce Watson, Benedict
Arnold, Jordan Freeman).

540ABE361854408D8B09BAFA7E8B2758.description:
Use evidence to develop a claim about the role of Connecticut in the American Revolution
(e.g., Provision State, privateers, Tory and Patriot sentiments).

80E4F8E0A7DD4EE192826FDEFADACBE2.description:
Explain probable causes and effects of major turning points in the American Revolution (e.g.,
Battle of Bunker Hill, Boston Massacre, Saratoga, Valley Forge).

EF37F7264CC64CC5BB57360EC9806A36.description:
Compare information provided by multiple historical sources about the people and events of
the American Revolution (e.g., purpose, maker, significance, fact, opinion, bias).

A37141F22A9B4E39BDFDA343E89E1AEF.description:
Describe how people’s perspectives of the American Revolution are documented in historical
records while noting representation of marginalized voices (e.g., journals, letters, newspaper
articles, pamphlets).

723AADD0EB1741969C62D5FC24A4B80B.description:
Explain why members of the Northeastern Woodland Native American tribes and Black
communities held conflicting views regarding support for the American Revolution.

FD77515E11B14E478B443A8B70B64021.description:
Explain how political and economic beliefs shaped the perspectives held by Patriots and
Loyalists leading to the American Revolution (e.g., individual rights, liberties, representation,
sovereignty, trade and taxation).

5D639EA909AC4E37863341C32AD51CD8.description:
Compare the benefits and costs of governmental and individual choices leading to the
American Revolution (e.g., taxation, homespun movement, right to property).

98977C75E70F47C0BEC8BFC025021A3C.description:
Employ chronological thinking to create timelines comparing the events that led to the
American Revolution (e.g., Seven Years War, Parliamentary acts of taxation, Boston Tea Party,
Boston Massacre, Declaration of Independence).

7012EEFC31B8434D93B65236591D978F.description:
Identify the civic virtues and democratic principles that contributed to the rejection of British
parliamentary rule of the North American colonies.

2A61282D0F7A454FAB13CA8A2A23F7D8.description:
Use evidence to develop a claim about a significant person, place, or event in Connecticut
during the Colonial Era (e.g., Pequot War, Connecticut Witch Trials, Charter Oak).

DE49570C1BC842649351CF379AE06B9A.description:
Compare how political systems were used to make rules that establish community leadership
and protect freedoms for various groups in the Colonial Era (e.g., town hall meetings, tribal
council, juries).

3C2A8C4CCF45426BBADE7D25050558A9.description:
Explain Connecticut’s connection to the transatlantic slave trade (e.g., New London’s deep
water ports, Wethersfield-constructed ship The Tryall).

3EE1ED5C419949A2BD20D9C780316914.description:
Describe resistance movements, both individual and group, against oppression in the
Colonial Era (e.g., Stono Rebellion, Pontiac Rebellion, New English Canaan).

BDF6A713D65D4581B626058852988E6B.description:
Analyze how the abilities and expertise that individuals from the African Diaspora brought
with them to the colonies contributed to economic specialization and trade (e.g., West African
rice cultivation, metal working, and basket weaving).

04301D474B7A4A08A1BD4CDFA785EB58.description:
Compare the reasons for different areas of specialization and trade among individuals and
businesses in New England, Middle, and Southern colonies (e.g., availability and access to
natural resources, hydropower, labor, trade routes).

EDE13D0A620545D794F940E593150A4D.description:
Identify examples of resources used to produce goods and services throughout colonial
settlements in the New England, Middle, and Southern regions (e.g., indentured and slave
labor, natural resources, tools, machines).

AA3238DDA895497D9CD066751F3831AA.description:
Summarize how the Fundamental Orders of Connecticut represented new ideas about
government (e.g., enfranchisement, representative government, consent of the governed).

080EAC9344DA47FAAA8067F3D27E21BF.description:
Explain how the desire for global power and influence led to the exploitation of colonies (e.g.,
Spanish galleon, Triangle Trade, Dutch East India Company, British East India Company).

AE28F2BA493A404EBF2CFF026AC13772.description:
Describe the role of money and currency in trade during the Colonial Era (e.g., British and
Spanish coins, tobacco, wampum, paper money).

C6AD1DB03BB4495596809F99135A7CF0.description:
Use maps to explain the relationship between the location of the New England, Middle,
and Southern colonies, and the environmental characteristics of each region (e.g., New
Amsterdam, New France, Jamestown, Plymouth, Saint Augustine).

25A6DA71ED2943AAB2B0FD8E9ADC142A.description:
Describe gender roles within and among Black, Indigenous, and European communities in
early United States history.

3773F9D2F79C4494817BDF81ED63E41B.description:
Explain how cultural diffusion of agricultural and technological knowledge held by African,
Indigenous, and European communities contributed to North American settlements (e.g., rice
cultivation, open field system, companion planting).

843B83FAFB4940D5A0B982D3766EFBA5.description:
Explain how the culture and experiences of African, Indigenous, and European people
influenced their perspectives during the Age of Exploration (e.g., cultural norms, political
beliefs, trade motives, exploitation).

CE24DA58C20A44E1B1CCD5BE1B216AC6.description:
Describe the causes and effects of European exploration and settlement of the Americas
(e.g., conflict, enslavement, land rights, sovereignty, trade).

1BA78A14C3A442E98DE29E858EEF4E9B.description: Describe the connection between natural resources and human settlement patterns in the Atlantic and Pacific Worlds (e.g., Caribbean, Europe, North America, South America, West Africa).

8267997FD0364CE3A1B77FF8D6B18060.description:
Explain probable causes and effects of the migration of Indigenous peoples and the
formation of Native nations in North America (e.g., archeological evidence).

5DCC71BDC30D463F9D4AFFEC9A2C6F74.description:
Use a range of deliberative and democratic procedures to evaluate and implement
strategies to address problems in classrooms and schools.

567DE763BAA24942B736CEDD2AB9A977.description:
Explain the challenges and opportunities, both present and past, in addressing local,

66AC38CF960845A1A160E48E0F45FADF.description:
Present a summary of arguments and explanations about early United States history using
print, oral, and digital technologies in classrooms, schools, and out-of-school contexts.

39B08DAA268A4C9694AC95EC47F2FA50.description:
Construct explanations using reasoning, correct sequence, examples, and details with
relevant information and data.

58FFFB953BFF4FFC9B1E87AD9E7CCA3B.description:
Construct arguments using claims and evidence from multiple sources about United
States history.

ECDF60AD20934E65BE5E2CA1ADB74793.description: Communicate Conclusions and Take Informed Action

A1F135D6CE4C4E55A0440AAB69F5C79F.description:
Use evidence to develop claims in response to a compelling question by using evidence
related to early United States history.

A8E6AAD1ED3A4274808F1D770FA4567C.description:
Identify evidence response to a compelling question while determining among fact and
opinion to determine the credibility of multiple sources.

FA078D58440B45279FD50A3C4C2699EE.description:
Gather relevant evidence from multiple sources about a person, event, or issue in United
States history while using the origin, structure, and context to guide selection.

CE7B42CFCA64404D8E4D07E4A784A60A.description:
Apply disciplinary knowledge and practices to demonstrate an understanding of United
States history content.

5ED8C71A9CE244C6A5D7F8A6AE79D586.description:
Determine the kinds of sources that will be helpful in answering compelling and
supporting questions, taking into consideration the different opinions people have about
how to answer the questions.

5C9599470A22472EB1C76FB2CF632CB8.description:
Explain how supporting questions help answer compelling questions in an inquiry about
United States history.

E8E49F0073C84F758F2C76B40BA5A28E.description:
Identify concepts, ideas, and interpretations associated with compelling and supporting
questions about early United States history.

Develop questions about historically significant regional and global economic events and
issues (e.g., European Sovereign Debt Crisis, Association of Southeast Asian Nations,
COVID-19 policy responses, Asia-Pacific Free Trade).

Explain the benefits and costs of trade policies to individuals and groups in a region (e.g.,
Belt and Road Initiative, Schengen Area, African Continental Free Trade Area).

88E22CB5276F4BE1B9F92702CF1155FB.description:

533A29813BF94005A1F2DBBDF8DEB9BA.description:
Explain how cultural patterns influence the environment and daily life within and among

62464B40212A412995F4637316B73C3D.description:

2346875DE656475685727E414E51AC53.description:
Demonstrate spatial awareness by constructing maps to represent spatial patterns and

Assess individual and collective capacities to take action to address local, regional, and

E699220CD7464D7388A6370C6175CB3C.description:
Analyze how a specific problem can manifest itself at local, regional, and global levels

4BB7017CA1E74F7694509682BDFCF2DF.description:
Present arguments and explanations about a local, regional, or global problem to reach a

26B727D0507647D19B20F514A10E9455.description:
Gather relevant evidence from multiple sources using both print and digital resources and

4DF50BB4BDA145F0BF2406AA4CC1E5B5.description:
Apply disciplinary knowledge and practices to demonstrate an understanding of world

677D88AB8DDE4CF88BBA0297AD1F7BAB.description:
Determine the kinds of sources that will be helpful in answering compelling and

800833EDA3424B0DBD1CD1A4FE794F01.description: Explain how compelling and supporting questions are mutually reinforcing.

1E75967F18CC437281A97421F8475078.description:
Explain how a trade barrier has shaped global or regional trade in historical and
contemporary contexts (e.g., tariff barrier, non-tariff barrier, embargo).

0EECD80741E34953B224871C8E6EDC87.description:
Explain how improvements in productivity enhance the standard of living in a region (e.g.,
automation, computer processing, 4-day workweek).

Describe tools and resources that are used to measure standard of living (e.g., Gross
Domestic Product, Human Development Index).

468DDB40C66143EBB45818E75AA20610.description:

A5843670978D4F14B9619B52E9CEEE67.description:

impact, advocacy).

Describe the role of competition in a market economy (e.g., prices, wages, tariffs, trade

CA0F5FC44F5D44B7AE385FE8DE2E3E69.description:

A1E45B21BD6D4BAC99FB8941720C5277.description:

54AD6AEBD9D44A4E9102BE85D3E64C03.description:

C3D97FC003804BC1BC26BABD07FB5438.description:

2AC12803CD0B4F0C916C0794426C5A5D.description:
Assess individual and collective capacities to take action to address local, regional, and
global problems, taking into account a range of possible levers of power, strategies, and

over time, identifying its characteristics and causes, and the challenges and opportunities
faced by those trying to address the problem.

document.title: Connecticut Elementary and Secondary Social Studies Standards

FBF0FAAE530744C98A05CE68856D45A1.description:
Evaluate the successes and failures of the Reconstruction in fulfilling ideas and principles
contained in the founding documents (e.g., elected Black officials, Ebenezer Bassett,
Freedmen’s Bureau, Historically Black Colleges and Universities, Compromise of 1877).

C1BE36E2D915488D91280408FC7D10A2.description:
Analyze the purposes, implementation, and consequences of policies and political strategies
during the Reconstruction Era (e.g., Homestead Act, Second Treaty of Fort Laramie, women’s
suffrage, Radical Reconstruction).

C837835C7CDA4328813BFE9986F7743C.description:
Explain multiple causes and effects of racism both during and after Reconstruction (e.g., Page
Act, Ku Klux Klan, Black Codes).

C420D488158A4B07BF77C8FE0FE1C94C.description:
Analyze the causes and effects of the Reconstruction Amendments (e.g., abolition, Latino and
Black citizenship, suffrage).

0F0A3A2C722548AEA51D8CEA58FEF2A0.description:
Explain how and why individuals challenged gender roles in the Civil War Era (e.g., Loreta
Janeta Velazquez, Frances Louisa Clayton, Anna Elizabeth Dickinson, Hartford Soldiers’ Aid
Society, Rebecca Primus and Addie Brown).

75B081F93A804458B70DF9A3FA621DF9.description:
Analyze the factors that shaped perspectives in Connecticut about the Civil War (e.g., free
labor movement, role of government, abolition).

A65718F3181149FBB73D92AA212F7871.description:
Analyze factors that influenced individual and group perspectives about national identity
both during and as a result of the Civil War (e.g., Copperheads, Republicans, Wide Awakes,
Unionists, women in the industrial workforce).

E2B50CEC7DB140D89C365A1310161E20.description:
Describe how policies related to military service shaped the events and outcomes of the
Civil War (e.g., conscription, Emancipation Proclamation, draft riots, Connecticut 29th,
Massachusetts 54th).

DB09354F14AA4CA9A4EE220CA56CF47B.description:
Explain how change and continuity in technology, infrastructure, and military strategies
shaped the Civil War (e.g., rail, scorched earth, blockade, Colt Firearms, Sharps Rifles).

6FE9C268531542298B4720A0451BDAD0.description:
Compare historical means used by individuals and groups to promote, sustain, and dismantle
discrimination in the Antebellum Period (e.g., Underground Railroad, Bleeding Kansas,
American Anti-Slavery Society, American Colonization Society, Compromise of 1850).

16874A5D04414A48B1570934E8BC231C.description:
Evaluate the relative influence of political, economic, and social developments that
contributed to secession (e.g., Free Soil Movement, Nullification, Dred Scott Decision,
Harper’s Ferry, abolition).

3E89374BF99C40109A46B33C0AE228A1.description:
Using multiple historical sources, identify individuals and groups during the Antebellum
Period who sustained, promoted, or challenged the institution of slavery (e.g., Frederick
Douglass, Harriett Beecher Stowe, John C. Calhoun).

8489F5CA3F04489D9479EBE8414FBE1E.description:
Analyze how secession sought to preserve the social, economic, and racial hierarchies
throughout the United States (e.g., domestic labor, manufacturing, slavocracy, textiles).

FE7FB8373DBA4B04B3888E0B6BC3E97A.description: Civil Unrest, Civil War, and Reconstruction

1B03563A5C574538B5748214E57DAF03.description:
Analyze the role of innovation and entrepreneurship at the start of the American Industrial
Revolution (e.g., mills, patents, telegraph, interchangeable parts).

B6D10057696B47C69A2983AE113A695B.description:
Explain how the demand for finished goods influenced business specialization and the
growing need for labor during the American Industrial Revolution (e.g., textiles, firearms,
shipbuilding, manufacturing, foundries, logging).

F1F689818D0242DB859D867F8540BA85.description:
Explain how the transition from an agricultural-based economy to an industrialized economy
affected the well-being of individuals, groups, and businesses (e.g., factory workers, child
laborers, women in the industrial workforce, formerly enslaved persons, Irish, Chinese, Black,
and White laborers and tradespeople).

B0C591A2F1CB4E099935A60D784C9659.description:
Explain how Westward Expansion increased access to natural resources and the production
and distribution of goods in a global market (e.g., agriculture, mining, canals, factories, rail,
shipping).

785FAA7CC1564C108E70DB3CE4677DA0.description:
Evaluate the influence human-induced environmental change had on spatial patterns of
industrialization and Westward Expansion (e.g., Cumberland and National Roads, Erie Canal,
Farmington Canal, Pacific Railroad).

B93B04E033C54D7E81D31D45D58505AC.description:
Compare movements for social change and the strategies they employed by the United States
in the Antebellum Period (e.g., abolition, Second Great Awakening, suffrage, temperance).

3EAA6D920126424EA49F887871C792DB.description:
Analyze attempts by individuals and groups with nativist views to shape the United States in
the Antebellum Period (e.g., Philadelphia Riots of 1844, Know Nothing Party).

C64B44EDE6E346A696F003B0E1E1B953.description:
Explain the causes and effects of government policies and executive decisions related to
industrialization and expansion of the United States (e.g., Bureau of Indian Affairs, Indian
Removal Act, Louisiana Purchase, Mexican-American War).

82C74FBD7ACD4A85859F440E6AC528E4.description:
Develop questions using multiple historical sources about how individuals and groups in
northern states sustained or challenged racial inequality during the Antebellum Period (e.g.,
Connecticut’s gradual emancipation act, Amistad Trials, Sarah Harris and Prudence Crandall,
The Liberator, American Colonization Society, American Anti-Slavery Society, Underground
Railroad).

E73F21A4FF10414D8529746DCC1DE06B.description:
Analyze the perspectives of immigrant groups and their reasons for moving to and within the
United States (e.g., German, Irish, Scandinavian, Chinese, Jewish).

87066077AAF14D558F38DCFC720B6CED.description:
Develop questions to analyze the significance of the methods of resistance employed by
enslaved and free Black people in the United States (e.g., work resistance, violence, sabotage,
petition, forming maroon communities, independent churches, and educational associations).

DBC08724926941888481D013A2DC076F.description:
Analyze the events and developments related to the institution of slavery in the early republic
(e.g., Haitian Revolution, Act Prohibiting the Importation of Slaves, cotton gin, textile industry).

E96999C587714A8EB56D947818E2A584.description:
Analyze the impact of United States’ treaties on the sovereignty of Native nations (e.g.,
Ordinance of 1787, Treaty of the Creeks, Treaty of Greenville, Louisiana Purchase, Treaty of
Fort Wayne).

9A9DE35D9FCF401BAE14A4FD9FACD4F7.description:
Evaluate the US Constitution and Bill of Rights to determine if the goals of the American
Revolution, as stated in the Declaration of Independence, were realized.

40D89B2A623944569ECA0CCB678EC6BE.description:
Explain the relevance of democratic principles in shaping acts of dissent and resistance in
early United States history (e.g., Whiskey Rebellion, Shay’s Rebellion, Nat Turner’s Rebellion).

5D5C43134F864884BB2764AE48B7EA91.description:
Analyze how ideas and principles about citizenship and access to political power expressed
in founding documents influenced social and political systems in the early republic (e.g., Bill
of Rights, Declaration of Independence, Three-Fifths Clause, Electoral College).

70B63A90B06A48BF9523221DA5818A69.description:
Analyze how the ideas and principles within the Bill of Rights influence the social and political
system in the United States.

789A5C0BE6B64EFBAAE74D1B4B5E4196.description:
Explain the perspectives, civic virtues, and democratic principles debated during the
Constitutional Convention (e.g., Connecticut Compromise, federalism, Three-Fifths
Compromise).

8B7AEE52B0CC42198E2ED4B66F64F58B.description:
Explain the evolving powers and limits of the three branches of government as defined in the
United States Constitution and subsequent federal court rulings, legislation, and executive
action (e.g., Alien and Sedition Acts, Marbury v. Madison, Treaty of San Lorenzo).

5C1CD38AA88A4859A18902AA530CF9F2.description:
Examine the origin, purpose, and impact of the founding documents (e.g., popular
sovereignty, republicanism, separation of powers, enfranchisement, liberty).

F5842CC07D8B44EDB2B7BDEC04829EF3.description:
Explain laws that institutionalized slavery in the Colonial Era and in the Constitution (e.g.,
Black Laws of Virginia, Fugitive Slave Act, Three-Fifths Clause).

14913B00CAB84E03B3E8037631883433.description:
Describe how individual and group perspectives of the American Revolution are documented
in historical records while identifying representation of marginalized voices (e.g., journals,
letters, pamphlets, newspaper articles from sources such as the Hartford Daily Courant).

7F4AD188C865497384E5033F296B16A3.description:
Analyze factors that influenced perspectives about national identity both during and as a
result of the American Revolution (e.g., social contract, individual liberties, tyranny, economic
and political sovereignty, citizenship).

BFB690A1A1CF477DBBDADE82E6F3343E.description:
Analyze the perspectives of both enslaved and free Black people through the historical
sources they created (e.g., Venture Smith, Phyllis Wheatley, Olaudah Equiano).

EE21F928B81A4872B7A52238E4CE1A4E.description:
Explain the events and developments that led to the establishment of colonies in the Atlantic
and Pacific Worlds (e.g., desire for religious liberty, natural resources, economic opportunities,
technological advancements).

3EEACEECC09D44A3B64640484275FBED.description: Origins of United States Democracy and National Identity

6516BA7303B042E18956DABD81400724.description:
Apply a range of deliberative and democratic procedures to make decisions and take
action in classrooms, schools, and out-of-school civic contexts.

D4E7E8AAA9D847EEB77789B366E342CB.description:
Analyze how a specific problem can manifest itself at local, regional, and global levels over
time, identifying its characteristics and causes, and the challenges and opportunities faced
by those trying to address the problem.

F7A9711879F14985B80DC6009E2EA347.description:
Present arguments and explanations that feature multiple perspectives about local, state,
or national history to reach a target audience using print, oral, and digital technologies.

FE415B4B46294ADFB50C748B740F78A0.description:
Critique the credibility of arguments and structure of explanations related to a historical
account of an event or issue in United States history.

D24777DA97424C2891CCA9FC7B91E72B.description:
Construct explanations using reasoning, summary, sequence, examples, and data while
pointing out the strengths and weaknesses of the explanations.

CB10724E7E244A5FA2925AD75E6DFAAE.description:
Construct arguments using evidence from multiple sources, while acknowledging the
strengths and limitations of the arguments.

190E4DD5A24543939F7DDCFB640A50EF.description: Communicate Conclusions and Take Informed Action

11ECE993BBB4415D9A518DC4965069F0.description:
Develop claims and counterclaims while pointing out the strengths and limitations of
different sources.

95D4E7EF651C4EF8B3446B611E37894B.description: Organize and prioritize relevant evidence from and among multiple sources to support claims.

C7A3E8BDCE02432FBA742D630BC751A5.description:
Gather information from multiple sources and evaluate their relevance and intended use
(e.g., origin, authority, structure, context, corroborative value, credibility).

6515949F056A4CB78616752D079F88B9.description:
Apply disciplinary knowledge and practices to demonstrate an understanding of United
States history content.

08F25763290240AC91FA8DFB1E9C8907.description:
Determine the kinds of sources that will be helpful in answering compelling and supporting
questions, taking into consideration multiple points of views represented in the sources.

CB3966E6394F4C40AD831881BCCF871E.description: Develop compelling and supporting questions that are mutually reinforcing.

EF2E8439EADB4B05A87A965C4DB423D6.description:
Explain how compelling and supporting questions represent key ideas in the study of
United States history.

document.title: Connecticut Elementary and Secondary Social Studies Standards

2A11C165CAF444F4B027509368E67C76.description:
Evaluate the role of various media platforms such as television, newspapers, and social
media in shaping reactions to events (e.g., Vietnam War, Tiananmen Square, fall of the
Berlin Wall, Arab Spring, Russo-Ukrainian War, 2016 and 2020 U.S. Presidential Elections).

7C2DA81AAD7A4EA3A16A54D84BD22917.description:
Explain how free-trade alliances and agreements have affected economic growth
in different nations in the late 20th century and 21st century (e.g., standard of living,
e-commerce, intellectual property, outsourcing, multinational organizations).

F5CBDA35BE074E0A92C0DB6F5A5E8335.description:
Analyze the role of comparative advantage in international trade in the late 20th century
and early 21st century (e.g., natural resources, labor availability, infrastructure, capital
goods, climate).

2ECD0E38C7404D559238963C08BBE4CD.description:
Describe an international economic policy in terms of intended and unintended market
outcomes (e.g., sanctions, free trade agreements, tariffs).

BA44E46B393744AF87A0E3C1B2D73022.description:
Analyze national and international responses to refugee crises sparked by natural
disasters, war, and genocide (e.g., Ukraine, Syria, Rohingya, Somalia, Latin America).

3253827EF3F54C97BDA35037D6E61CDD.description:
Analyze how individuals and groups advocate for economic, political, and social change
in international contexts (e.g., legislation, courts, resistance, protest, boycott, conscious
consumerism).

5CD33EE71B0F4F6C9221F75E5E5AC66D.description:
Evaluate the effectiveness of the international organizations in sustaining or undermining
global cooperation (League of Nations, United Nations, Organization of the Petroleum
Exporting Countries, North Atlantic Treaty Organization, European Union, Asia-Pacific
Economic Cooperation, International Court of Justice, Community of Latin American and
Caribbean States).

A0D3C24EBB74406E96B01D11B504188D.description:
Evaluate how economic globalization and the expanding use of scarce resources has led
to conflict and cooperation within and among nations and international organizations (e.g.,
Role of International Monetary Fund austerity policy in Jamaica, 2003 invasion of Iraq,
Annexation of Crimea, African Union, Central America-Dominican Republic Free Trade
Agreement, International Group of Seven).

1BEF9A62DFE548C6B845DC07F1FCDD6C.description:
Evaluate the influence of long-term climate variability on contemporary human migration,
settlement patterns, resource use, and land use at local-to-global scales (e.g., heat waves,
desertification, loss of biodiversity, fish migration, irrigation, wildfires).

0D9A39D26E54411F9D6217FBA06EEC7A.description:
Evaluate how the growth of the global economy has led to changes in settlement patterns
(e.g., urbanization, resource scarcity, immigration, emigration, war, industrial waste).

28975C0BB22D435696CACA100A4C104C.description:
Evaluate the multinational political and economic agreements that have led to changes in
cultural and environmental characteristics among and within nations (e.g., European Union,
Kyoto Protocol, Paris Agreement, North American Free Trade Agreement, Trans-Pacific
Partnership, International Monetary Fund).

E90812FE2C73443ABFDD0DD79D62AF69.description:
Analyze the multiple and complex causes and effects of national and global public health
issues (e.g., HIV/AIDS, Ebola, reproductive health, addiction, climate change, nutrition,
potable water, COVID pandemic).

BBB9B3741B90432880AC23F2360B9AE2.description:
Develop questions about strategies used to promote and extend human rights and their
significance in both historical and contemporary global contexts (e.g., litigation, lobbying,
protests, social media, economic sanctions, diplomacy).

20ADF210668F41B5A6CD9730F8BF8484.description:
Analyze the impact of scientific and technological change in the late 20th and early 21st
century (e.g., International Space Station, computer technology, vaccines and public health,
Global Positioning Systems, cellular technology, Artificial Intelligence).

CF653F4241DB4487A310B85F9689D9A0.description:
Analyze historical and contemporary examples of the formation, dissolution or restructuring
of governments (e.g., Soviet Union, Israel, Republic of Iran, Zaire, Cuban Revolution,
Sandinista National Liberation Front).

52C90FC6A03C41AA9CEAE5298B1D3A15.description:
Analyze means of protecting or limiting human rights in the 20th century (e.g., Universal
Declaration of Human Rights, United Nations Resolution 181, Partition of India, Dirty War in
Argentina, Cultural Revolution in China, Khmer Rouge, Stolen Generations in Australia).

8CC8A21864E8476F801434DBB0AD8368.description:
Analyze the impact of treaties and laws on the maintenance of national and international
order in the 20th century (e.g., Apartheid, European Economic Community, Camp David
Accords, Sino-American Mutual Defense Treaty, Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty, Latin
American Integration Association).

AF4DC1108B25430DBECB68D23AB084EA.description:
Analyze how developments in multimedia shaped the perspectives of individuals
and groups in the 20th century (e.g., comic books, communication technologies, film,
propaganda, public service announcements, radio).

262CFA96225A4DF5B10EEEEDF1E86AA2.description:
Analyze the complex and interacting factors that led to genocide during different historical
eras (e.g., Armenia, Uganda, Cambodia, Bosnia, Rwanda, Darfur).

7C544FEBD4A94569BD02629BEF44F84F.description:
Analyze complex and interacting factors that influenced the perspectives about
international laws and treaties in the Cold War era (e.g., United Nations, Geneva
Conventions, North Atlantic Treaty Organization, Warsaw Pact, Nuclear Non-Proliferation
Treaty).

14AF3EB3798544DCAF557C2BA570D631.description:
Examine ways in which decolonization altered the balance of power within and among
nations (e.g., independence movements, decline of European political imperialism,
economic imperialism, ascendency of United States and Soviet Union as leading world
powers).

11DCECC0F4CD4F6CB5D10500644D91C4.description:
Evaluate how resistance movements and decolonization were shaped by post-World War II
circumstances and broader historical contexts (e.g., India, Kenya, Vietnam, Korea, Algeria,
Indonesia, Hungary, Germany).

76D7E42C078B47938D8426DE0734A429.description:
Analyze how changes in military technology impacted the outcomes of various conflicts
throughout the 20th century (e.g., barbed wire, bio-chemicals, flamethrowers, submarines,
tanks, aircraft, computer technology, nuclear weapons).

5FA8C7AA4036498D816A36E52DEADA3A.description:
Develop a historical argument about the long-term causes and triggering events that led
to World War II (e.g., militarism, nationalism, Treaty of Versailles, Japanese imperialism,
appeasement).

27570751C0E34A4A89BAD87AE7643CAA.description:
Synthesize sources from the Holocaust to develop questions and explore the experiences
of survivors, victims, resisters, collaborators, bystanders, and rescuers (e.g., survivor
testimony, memoirs, government documents, museums exhibits, historical fiction, and film).

4283428F6FE6444B8FB37E23D12B2226.description:
Investigate the ways in which antisemitic beliefs and other discriminatory policies in Europe
led to the persecution and murder of millions of Jews as well as Roma, disabled people,
LGBTQ+ individuals, and political prisoners during the Holocaust (e.g., Nuremberg Race
Laws, Final Solution, Aktion T4).

8E421D24AA224C78B53DC538F9141FC6.description:
Evaluate how the causes and effects of World War I influenced global conflicts in the 20th
century (e.g., imperialism, industrialization, nationalism, collapse of empires, communism,
socialism, fascism).

D0CDEB70EDD644AF9EEA0133514E0D95.description:
Investigate how different groups have struggled to gain freedom, equality, and social
justice at the national and international levels (e.g., Nelson Mandela, Ho Chi Minh, Kwame
Nkrumah, Indian National Congress).

53B0B445E87F4ED7938E5D12BEAF1888.description:
Analyze how historical events during imperialism influenced migration patterns and
population distribution (e.g., Berlin Conference of 1884-1885, Royal Niger Company,
Monroe Doctrine, Battle of Port Arthur).

50D986145C4C4302A602C2B190F5B48C.description:
Explain the relationships between the locations of places and the impact of imperialism
using maps and other representations (e.g., social, cultural, economic, political).

A7BCBD6CEC614E4E85C8DFC1179DFBD8.description:
Analyze the complex and interacting cultural, religious, and racial factors that influenced
perspectives of imperialist policies (e.g., Rudyard Kipling, E. D. Morel, Dadabhai Naoroji,
Boxer Rebellion, Sepoy Rebellion).

897A3B4CF7C74C85932DCFEEBEA66EE8.description:
Evaluate how imperialism was shaped by rivalries between industrialized nation-states for
political and economic power (e.g., Japan, Great Britain, France, Belgium, Germany).

7431D8DB31954445B10BF8632780E9EA.description:
Analyze how access to resources resulted in imperialist policies that had a range of
costs and benefits for different groups (e.g., West African diamonds, Middle Eastern oil,
Congolese rubber, Indian spices, Panama Canal, Manchuria).

EAEFF7C106614BCFB1923F45F6C786DB.description:
Analyze how the Industrial Revolution impacted the balance of power among nations (e.g.,
Opium Wars, Sino-Japanese relations prior to and post the Meiji Reformation, Crimean War,
Zulu War, Mahdist War, Anglo-German naval arms race, Scramble for Africa).

E69C323FC4704D96BC8DF24338DD7663.description:
Evaluate how the cultural and environmental changes caused by industrialization
influenced spatial patterns of trade and land use (e.g., Enclosure Movement, Bombay
Spinning and Weaving Company, Treaty of Amity and Commerce, Suez Canal).

1B7EAB5AFA28417B977C8834293D796E.description:
Analyze the relationships and interactions between growing industry and physical systems
to explain reciprocal influences that occur among them (e.g., air pollution, hydropower,
mining, dredging).

CA862B67691E4551AE945512E9B178E7.description:
Analyze multiple and complex causes and effects of industrialization (e.g., geographic
features, technological innovations, access to capital, exploitative foreign policies and
impact on native populations, environmental degradation, population trends, labor
standards).

00B1017F66BF4F77863EDC6A6922C817.description:
Analyze how industrialization gave rise to new ideals and their related policies (e.g.,
laissez-faire, communism, feminism, socialism, utilitarianism, utopianism).

443F14A5A067439598B20C39B82BE2A5.description:
Analyze how theories of government developed in the Age of Enlightenment represented
new ideas about the balance between rights of the individual and power of the government.

2371D0302505464BBAD6B7E66BBE0148.description:
Evaluate the extent to which political and social change was advanced by women in the
Enlightenment and Scientific Revolution (e.g., Mary Wollstonecraft, Margaret Cavendish,
Maria Winkleman, Maria Merian).

7271F22D6BF342AB83C0F7C8924ECC41.description:
Demonstrate spatial awareness by creating maps to illustrate the environmental
characteristics and patterns of trade in early modern world history using digital technologies
(e.g., colonialism, enslavement, imperialism, revolution).

D25E770A4E324F0EA5F89C761A004917.description:
Analyze how the diffusion of Enlightenment ideas influenced revolutions (e.g., United States,
France, Haiti, Venezuela).

CF3AC58C330F47FD8D61E40C50A36D84.description:
Evaluate how the Enlightenment and Scientific Revolution shaped institutions in society
(e.g., deism, individual liberty, religious tolerance, reason, scientific method).

C4371CF1AF6E4138BFD98F19A4F8E7A9.description:
Describe how the Atlantic system affected global trade through cultural diffusion and
competition (e.g., de-emphasis of Silk Road, extraction of natural resources, growth of
transatlantic slave trade, colonization of the Americas).

ACDF982A4B5A44C8815D11DF2982D43C.description:
Evaluate the impact of settlement on the environmental and cultural characteristics of the
early modern world (e.g., hacienda, encomienda, Jesuit missionaries, East India Company,
Ottoman Empire, unification of Japan, Indigenous genocide).

5D02F2D15350413084EA699CD3D46063.description:
Analyze how current interpretations of cultural exchange of the early modern world are
limited by the availability of sources and the perspectives represented (e.g., accounts
by Gomes de Zurara, Conquistadors, Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq, Francisco de Almeida,
Bartolomé de las Casas, Francis Xavier).

A66BE025EF4F4E2AAE4DED0384A46BC3.description:
Evaluate how historical events and developments were shaped by the movement of
individuals and groups during maritime exploration (e.g., Treaty of Tordesillas, Seven
Voyages of Zheng He, Columbian exchange).

F2D05EA961654E068909AFD2C0D42953.description:
Evaluate and implement strategies for individual and collective action to address global
problems in classrooms, schools, and out-of-school civic contexts.

03E848D06BAD4B5A9A2DC9EE84FD9C21.description:
Analyze the characteristics and causation of ongoing global problems, both past and
present, using a multidisciplinary lens.

A30972C352CC45E09CE45783C41F2CE0.description:
Present arguments and explanations that feature evocative ideas and multiple
perspectives about modern world history topics to reach a range of audiences and
venues outside the classroom using print, oral, and digital technologies.

A86A8CB3786A4D40B20B7CF73BBD0112.description:
Critique historical arguments and explanations while acknowledging the strengths
and weaknesses given the purpose and audience (e.g., credibility, bias, reasoning,
sequencing, details).

D8285A3AF90D40F392F7F19C8FAF5FF2.description:
Construct explanations using sound reasoning, correct sequence, relevant examples, and
pertinent details to contextualize evidence and arguments (e.g., chronology, causation,
procedure).

803A808AE8044CB08B2714B257A220FC.description:
Construct arguments using precise and knowledgeable claims, with evidence from
multiple sources, while acknowledging counterclaims and evidentiary weaknesses.

Gather relevant information from multiple sources representing a wide range of views
and mediums while using the origin, authority, structure, context, and corroborative value
